title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
feed_text:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

Via Hacker News

Tags: computer-history, game-design, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, ai-ethics, coding-agents

title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
feed_text:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic

Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.

When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied:

Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.

As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

Via Hacker News

Tags: git, migrations, version-control, ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, agentic-engineering

title: llm-gemini 0.35
feed_text:
Release: llm-gemini 0.35

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist!

Tags: google, ai, generative-ai, llms, llm, gemini, llm-pricing, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, llm-release

title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
feed_text:
If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten.

— Geoffrey Huntley, nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left.

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
feed_text:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

Explicit lazy imports

I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.

Unpacking in comprehensions

The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:

lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}

PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.

A sampling profiler

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.

I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.

If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):

sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234

Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.

3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.

Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.

Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv

I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:

uv self update

Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:

uv python install 3.15

And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:

uv python pin --global 3.15

Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:

uv run python --version

I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:

uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15

Then I can confirm the version like this:

datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq

Highlights from Python 3.11

The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.

My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.

Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!

Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.

datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.

Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:

  • setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
  • create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.
  • blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
  • You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system.

I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.

I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

Tags: open-source, profiling, python, sqlite, uv

.ghdiagram-html {
  --ghd-text: #1f2328;
  --ghd-muted: #5a615c;
  --ghd-canvas: #f2f5f3;
  --ghd-card: #ffffff;
  --ghd-border: #c4ccc6;
  --ghd-accent: #0fbf3e;
  --ghd-connector: #0b862b;
  --ghd-padding: 24px;
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 699px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  color: var(--ghd-text);
  font: 400 15px/22px "GH Diagram Sans", sans-serif;
  font-synthesis: none;
  font-optical-sizing: none;
  font-variation-settings: normal;
  font-variant-ligatures: none;
  letter-spacing: 0;
  text-align: left;
  -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
}
.ghdiagram-html *,
.ghdiagram-html *::before,
.ghdiagram-html *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
.ghdiagram-html [hidden] { display: none !important; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__canvas {
  padding: var(--ghd-padding);
  background: var(--ghd-canvas);
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__heading { display: grid; gap: 8px; margin-bottom: 28px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__title,
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node-title,
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__section-title {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
  border: 0;
  color: var(--ghd-text);
  font: 500 18px/26px "GH Diagram Sans", sans-serif;
  font-variation-settings: normal;
  letter-spacing: 0;
  text-transform: none;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__title { font-size: 32px; line-height: 40px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__eyebrow {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--ghd-muted);
  /* Match the timeline charts' eyebrow: Mona Sans (not Mono), tracked uppercase.
     The bundled Sans tops out at 500, so use that rather than faux-bolding to 700. */
  font-family: "GH Diagram Sans", sans-serif;
  font-size: clamp(12px, 1.5vw, 13px);
  font-weight: 500;
  line-height: 1.3;
  letter-spacing: 0.12em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  font-variation-settings: normal;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node-eyebrow {
  margin: -4px 0 -8px;
  color: var(--ghd-muted);
  font: 500 11px/16px "GH Diagram Sans", sans-serif;
  letter-spacing: 0.1em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__viewport { overflow-x: auto; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__viewport--fit { overflow: hidden; overflow: clip; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__viewport--fit > .ghdiagram-html__plane { transform-origin: 0 0; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__heading-meta {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
  gap: 8px 16px;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__header-badge {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 4px 8px;
  border-radius: 6px;
  box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--ghd-border);
  background: var(--ghd-card);
  color: var(--ghd-muted);
  font: 400 12px/16px "GH Diagram Mono", monospace;
  font-variation-settings: normal;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
/* Matches the charts' title/subtitle rhythm: an 8px grid gap less 6px. */
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__subtitle {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--ghd-muted);
  font: 400 15px/22px "GH Diagram Sans", sans-serif;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__title + .ghdiagram-html__subtitle { margin-top: -6px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__note {
  margin: 24px 0 0;
  color: var(--ghd-muted);
  font: 400 13px/20px "GH Diagram Sans", sans-serif;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__plane { position: relative; display: grid; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__row { display: grid; align-items: stretch; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__row--flow {
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, var(--ghd-flow-min-width, 180px)), 1fr));
}
/* Strokes are inset 1px rings, not outlines: WebKit snaps a half-pixel
   outline offset unevenly, so rounded corners looked doubled. */
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node {
  min-width: 0;
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1;
  padding: 24px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 8px;
  box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--ghd-border);
  background: var(--ghd-card);
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__content { display: grid; align-content: start; gap: 16px; min-width: 0; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node--annotation .ghdiagram-html__content { gap: 8px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node--dashed { box-shadow: none; outline: 1px dashed var(--ghd-border); outline-offset: -1px; }
.ghdiagram-html[data-ghd-state="ready"] .ghdiagram-html__node--dashed { outline: none; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node--accent { --ghd-title-size: 20px; border-radius: 0 0 8px 8px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node--accent::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0 0 auto;
  height: 3px;
  border-radius: 1.5px;
  background: var(--ghd-accent);
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node--accent .ghdiagram-html__node-title { font-size: 20px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node-heading { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px 12px; align-items: center; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__node-heading--stat { display: grid; gap: 4px; }
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__stat {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 10px;
  color: var(--ghd-emphasis, var(--ghd-accent));
  font-size: calc(var(--ghd-title-size, 18px) * var(--ghd-stat-scale, 2));
  font-weight: 500;
  line-height: 1.2;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__stat--up::after,
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__stat--down::after {
  content: "";
  display: block;
  width: 0;
  height: 0;
  flex: 0 0 auto;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__stat--up::after {
  border-right: 11px solid transparent;
  border-bottom: 18px solid currentColor;
  border-left: 11px solid transparent;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__stat--down::after {
  border-top: 18px solid currentColor;
  border-right: 11px solid transparent;
  border-left: 11px solid transparent;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__body {
  margin: 0;
  color: var(--ghd-muted);
  font: inherit;
  white-space: pre-line;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__chips {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  align-content: start;
  gap: 8px;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
  list-style: none;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__chip,
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__badge {
  display: block;
  max-width: 100%;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 5.5px 10px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 6px;
  box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px var(--ghd-stroke, var(--ghd-border));
  background: var(--ghd-canvas);
  color: var(--ghd-text);
  font: 400 14px/20px "GH Diagram Mono", monospace;
  font-variation-settings: normal;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__chip--dashed {
  box-shadow: none;
  outline: 1px dashed var(--ghd-stroke, var(--ghd-border));
  outline-offset: -1px;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__chip--icon {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: var(--ghd-icon-size, 16px) minmax(0, 1fr);
  align-items: start;
  gap: 8px;
}
.ghdiagram-html .ghdiagram-html__chip--icon .ghdiagram-html__icon { color: inherit; }

<html><body><p class="wp-block-paragraph">Secret scanning works best when developers are confident in the findings. Catch too little, and real credentials can remain in a repository. Alert too often, and developers may spend time investigating strings that aren’t secrets.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Generic secrets make that balance especially difficult. The same string could be a real credential or a documentation placeholder, so detecting it requires understanding the surrounding code and text.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">To address this challenge, we trained a secret classifier specifically for GitHub’s product needs: distinguishing real credentials from lookalikes while meeting the speed and efficiency requirements of scanning at scale.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In our companion post, <a href="https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/secret-protection-must-scale-with-software/"><strong>Secret protection must scale with software</strong></a>, we explained why secret protection must keep pace with AI-accelerated development. Here, we go behind the scenes of the context-aware classifier powering that effort: how we designed, trained, and evaluated it to find more real secrets with less noise.</p>



<h2 id="h-what-we-enabled" class="wp-block-heading">What we enabled</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">GitHub secret scanning operates at two key moments:</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Push protection</strong> helps prevent secrets from entering a repository by scanning changes before a push is accepted, giving developers an opportunity to address the finding.</li>



<li><strong>Post-push scanning</strong> works after code has been committed, continuously scanning repository content and creating alerts when potential secrets are detected so developers and security teams can investigate and remediate them.</li>
</ul>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We developed a fast classifier that reduced median post-push scan execution time by 86% compared with the previous LLM-based pipeline. That efficiency made it practical to extend generic secret detection to push protection, returning results before developers push changes, not only after code is committed.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-video"><video height="2160" style="aspect-ratio: 2778 / 2160;" width="2778" controls src="https://github.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/UI-1.mp4"></video><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><em>Secret scanning blocks a commit</em> <em>with push protection after the model detects a secret on line 5 of the file.</em></figcaption></figure>



<h2 id="h-why-secrets-are-hard-to-detect" class="wp-block-heading">Why secrets are hard to detect</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Structured credentials often include a distinctive prefix, length, alphabet, or checksum. Generic secrets may not. Their syntax overlaps with build identifiers, checksums, asset hashes, sample values, and other non-sensitive strings. Context is the deciding signal.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><thead><tr><th><strong>Likely real credential</strong></th><th><strong>Likely harmless lookalike</strong></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>A password assigned beside a production database URL</td><td>The same password-shaped value in a test fixture</td></tr><tr><td>A connection string in deployment configuration</td><td>A localhost connection string in a setup guide</td></tr><tr><td>A high-entropy value bound to an API credential</td><td>A high-entropy checksum, build ID, or asset hash</td></tr></tbody></table></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">These cases are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Adding more rules can suppress some of them, but each exception risks hiding a real secret. A learned classifier can instead use signals such as file path, secret type, variable names, and nearby code or text.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That is why we shipped a new scanner using a two-stage pipeline:</p>



<ol class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Candidate generation</strong>: Regex filters scan content for potential secrets with high recall. This stage is optimized to catch broad families of credential-like patterns quickly and deterministically.</li>



<li><strong>Context-aware classification</strong>: A fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates each candidate and its surrounding context. It is trained to recognize the signals that separate real secrets from false positives, including placeholder values, examples, documentation snippets, generated content, and non-sensitive identifiers. Because the model is small and efficient to run on our inference infrastructure, it costs much less to serve and is simpler to scale than an LLM-based pipeline.</li>
</ol>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Impact:</strong></p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>11.5% user acceptance improvement, reducing false positives.</li>



<li>86% faster post-push secret detection execution time.</li>



<li>More than 98% cost savings compared with the LLM-based pipeline.</li>
</ul>



<h2 id="h-how-our-pipeline-works" class="wp-block-heading">How our pipeline works</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">As content is scanned, regex patterns cast a wide net and flag anything that looks like a credential, so real secrets aren’t missed at the start. Each candidate then goes to a fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier, which reads the value together with its file path, variable names, and surrounding code. The classifier estimates how likely it is to be a real secret. High-confidence findings become alerts, and lookalikes such as placeholders, test fixtures, and checksums are filtered out before they reach developers.</p>

HOW OUR PIPELINE WORKS

STEP 1

<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The important design choice is that the model does not replace deterministic scanning. Instead, it complements it. Regexes remain the right tool for finding candidate strings quickly. The classifier is used where machine learning provides the most leverage: distinguishing “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”</p>



<figure class="wp-block-video"><video height="2160" style="aspect-ratio: 3070 / 2160;" width="3070" controls src="https://github.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/list-view-blog.mp4"></video><figcaption class="wp-element-caption"><em><em>The classifier model makes a best effort to distinguish “looks like a secret” from “is likely a real secret.”</em></em></figcaption></figure>



<h2 id="h-a-hard-negative-problem-secrets-that-almost-look-real" class="wp-block-heading">A hard-negative problem: secrets that almost look real</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Most false positives are not random. They are hard negatives: strings that match a credential pattern but are not usable credentials. Examples include documentation placeholders, toy examples in tests, redacted values, non-sensitive IDs, and generated fixtures. These cases are easy for a regex to match and hard for a purely rule-based system to suppress without accidentally losing real secrets.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">ModernBERT helps because it can read the candidate together with nearby code and text providing contextual understanding comparable to an LLM without the latency and computational overhead of generating natural-language output. For example, a candidate surrounded by words like “example,” “dummy,” “fake,” or “replace-me” may be lower risk than a candidate assigned to an environment variable in a deployment file. The classifier learns these contextual differences from labeled examples rather than requiring engineers to encode every exception as another rule.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We chose ModernBERT because it provides a strong fit for this workload: it is compact, efficient, and well suited for classification over code-adjacent text. For secret scanning, the model needs to make a calibrated decision over short candidate windows with high throughput and low latency.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">That makes a fine-tuned encoder classifier a better serving shape than a general-purpose LLM for this stage of the pipeline. The model can be trained directly on our decision boundary, and evaluated using the same recall and precision metrics that matter to secret scanning quality.</p>



<h2 id="h-how-we-trained" class="wp-block-heading">How we trained</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The challenge was finding representative data for cases in which syntax alone is misleading. The training and evaluation strategy combines three sources: </p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Product-derived examples from GitHub repositories, using feedback from the secret detection experience and additional human validation.</li>



<li>High-recall regex candidates from GitHub repository data, including human-annotated examples and weak labels used to expand coverage.</li>



<li>Synthetic examples targeted at sparse and difficult cases, such as documentation secrets, test fixtures, public keys, checksums, structured lookalikes, and near-miss pairs.</li>
</ul>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Synthetic rows pass deterministic validation and model-based quality review before inclusion. Training emphasizes real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that frequently confuse regex-only approaches. Each model input includes the candidate value, file path, secret type, and a bounded amount of surrounding context. We select thresholds through offline evaluation and then validate behavior on production-like traffic before broader rollout.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Before splitting the data, we grouped rows that share a repository, candidate value, or example so near-duplicates could not appear in both training and evaluation.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Training focused on the cases that matter most for alert quality: real secrets, realistic false positives, and hard negatives that regexes frequently match. The input representation includes the candidate secret string, file path, type and a bounded amount of surrounding context. The output is a classification score used by the scanner to decide whether the candidate should proceed.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We optimized for the product tradeoff: preserve or improve recall while reducing false positives and serving cost. In practice, that means the classifier threshold is selected using offline evaluation, then validated against production-like traffic before rollout.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The most important training principle was to make the model see the confusing examples. We included candidates that are syntactically similar to real secrets but semantically different, so the model learns not only what a secret looks like, but also what a false positive looks like in context.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 8-bit quantization, enabling fast inference.</p>



<h2 id="h-evaluation-results" class="wp-block-heading">Evaluation results</h2>



<figure class="wp-block-table"><table class="has-fixed-layout"><thead><tr><th><strong>Online result</strong></th><th><strong>Change vs. previous LLM pipeline</strong></th><th><strong>What it measures</strong></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Repository owner-weighted acceptance </td><td><strong>11.5% higher</strong> </td><td>Customer acceptance of detected findings </td></tr><tr><td>Median post-push scan execution time </td><td><strong>86% lower</strong> </td><td>Production scan execution time </td></tr><tr><td>Serving cost </td><td><strong>More than 98% lower</strong> </td><td>Cost of the compact classifier compared with remote LLM calls </td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Customer A/B evaluation results for our fine-tuned model compared to the previous LLM pipeline.</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We evaluated the new pipeline’s impact in production in two stages: first against the production baseline on the same public traffic and then through a customer A/B experiment. </p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li><strong>Offline evaluation:</strong> On post-push scanning, the new pipeline achieved <strong>13% higher precision and 19% higher recall</strong> than the previous LLM pipeline when evaluated on the same public traffic. </li>



<li><strong>Online evaluation:</strong> We then validated whether these quality improvements translated to customer outcomes through an A/B experiment against the previous LLM pipeline. <strong>Repository owner-weighted acceptance increased by 11.5%.</strong> We weight acceptance by repository owner to reduce the influence of customers who bulk-resolve large volumes of alerts at once, which can otherwise distort a simple average. </li>
</ul>



<h2 id="h-take-this-with-you" class="wp-block-heading">Take this with you</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The best security tool is the one developers trust enough to use. Higher precision means fewer distracting alerts. Higher recall means more real secrets are caught. Lower cost means we can keep improving coverage without making scanning prohibitively expensive.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For developers and security teams, this should translate into fewer false positives, and faster feedback in the places where secrets are most likely to be introduced: commits, pull requests, and everyday development workflows.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Hybrid systems are powerful. Regex gives us speed, transparency, and broad candidate coverage. ModernBERT gives us learned context understanding and false-positive reduction. The combination outperforms either approach used alone for this product constraint.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">We also learned that model size is not the same as model usefulness. A smaller fine-tuned classifier can be the right answer when the task is narrow, the decision boundary is measurable, and serving efficiency is critical.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">This is one step toward making secret scanning more accurate, scalable, and easy to use. Looking ahead, we are focused on two areas:</p>



<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Building a continuous improvement flywheel. We will use production feedback loops to identify new false negatives and false positives, turning real-world signals into higher-quality training and evaluation data.</li>



<li>Exploring new model architectures. We are investigating approaches that can perform secret detection and extraction in a single step, reducing pipeline complexity while preserving accuracy and scale.</li>
</ul>



<h2 id="h-acknowledgments" class="wp-block-heading">Acknowledgments</h2>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Huge thanks to the engineering, science and product teams across GitHub and Microsoft who helped build the training data, evaluation suite, serving stack, and rollout plan for this new secret scanner.</p>
</body></html>
<p>The post <a href="https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/githubs-model-for-secret-detection-finding-more-secrets-with-less-noise/">GitHub’s model for secret detection: Finding more secrets with less noise</a> appeared first on <a href="https://github.blog">The GitHub Blog</a>.</p>

title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase
feed_text:
Context matters when you’re working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types.

Copilot can help you make changes across a project, but it works best when it knows those rules, too. Much of that knowledge can live inside the repository, so Copilot can pick it up automatically instead of requiring you to explain the same standards, scripts, and workflows every time you start a new task.

In this installment of our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series, we’ll look at four ways to tailor how Copilot works with your project:

  • Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow.
  • Agent skills package repeatable procedures.
  • Custom agents bring specialized guidance to larger tasks.
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connect Copilot to external tools and data sources, expanding what it can do.

Let’s look at how each one works and how they can work together.

Start with custom instructions

Suppose you ask Copilot to add a custom page size to an application. Making the change is only part of the job. The new code should also follow the patterns your team already uses.

Repository custom instructions give Copilot that baseline context. Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation.

You can also create path-specific instruction files inside .github/instructions. These files use an applyTo field to tell Copilot when the guidance is relevant.

When Copilot works on a matching file, it can use both the repository-wide instructions and the more specific guidance. That lets you keep the broad rules in one place without forcing every file type into the same mold.

Package repeatable procedures as agent skills

Custom instructions are useful for standards that should shape many tasks. But some guidance only matters when Copilot is performing a particular procedure, such as running quality checks, preparing a release, or debugging a failed workflow.

That’s where agent skills come in. A skill is a folder containing instructions and, optionally, scripts and other resources that Copilot can load when they’re relevant. Project-level skills can live in .github/skills, with each skill in its own subfolder.

For example, a .github/skills/quality-checks folder could contain a SKILL.md file that explains:

  • When Copilot should use the skill.
  • Which scripts run the project’s tests and linting.
  • What each script checks.
  • How to troubleshoot common failures.

The description in SKILL.md helps Copilot determine when the skill applies. After updating the interface, Copilot can load the quality-checks skill and follow the project’s established process for testing and linting instead of guessing which commands to run.

Use a custom agent for broader, specialized work

Some tasks are larger than a single procedure. An accessibility review, for example, may require Copilot to inspect components, templates, styles, and interactions across multiple files.

Custom agents let you create specialized versions of Copilot for work like this. A repository-level agent profile lives in .github/agents and can define the agent’s purpose, instructions, tools, and relevant project context.

Use a custom agent when a recurring type of work benefits from a dedicated role or perspective, especially when the task may span multiple files and draw on several tools or sources of context.

Connect Copilot to external tools with MCP servers

Instructions, skills, and agents help Copilot understand how to work within your project. MCP servers expand what it can access and do beyond the repository.

MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, data sources, and services. A documentation server can give it access to framework guidance, while a server such as Playwright can let it open and interact with your application in a browser.

You can browse available MCP servers in the Copilot app or add a custom one. Once Playwright is configured, you can ask: Use the Playwright MCP server to test the functionality manually.

Copilot can then use Playwright to open the application in a browser and interact with it much as you would. That gives it a way to verify not only that the code passes automated checks, but also that the updated interface behaves as expected.

Choose the right type of customizations

These customizations solve different problems, but they become more useful when you combine them:

  • Custom instructions define the conventions Copilot should follow across the repository or for particular files.
  • Agent skills package repeatable procedures that Copilot can load when they’re relevant.
  • Custom agents provide focused expertise and guidance for broader tasks.
  • MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, services, and data sources, expanding what Copilot can do.

Take this with you

Giving Copilot useful project context starts with four questions:

  • What project convention do I keep explaining?
  • What multi-step procedure do I repeat?
  • What complex task could benefit from a dedicated custom agent?
  • What outside tool or source does Copilot need?

Not sure where to begin? The community has shared ready-made instructions, skills, agents, and more through Awesome Copilot. Find one that addresses a workflow you already repeat, review what it contains, and adapt it to your repository’s tools and standards.

Start small: choose one convention you keep explaining, add it to .github/copilot-instructions.md, and see how Copilot applies it to your next task.

Try using the GitHub Copilot app >

The post GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

title: Secret protection must scale with software
feed_text:
Today, one in three pull requests on GitHub involves an AI agent. A year ago, that number was fewer than one in 10. If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human.

If developers and agents move faster, we have a responsibility to ensure protection keeps up with the accelerated rate of code creation. That means preventing more leaks before they happen and making the response to exposures that remain less dependent on manual human effort.

This is a pivotal point for leaked secrets. Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it.

In this essay, I share the nine quarters of data behind that claim. I also introduce the fine-tuned classifier we built with Microsoft Applied Sciences to extend push protection to unstructured secrets. The model assesses a whole set of candidate secrets in less than two milliseconds and could more than double the number of secrets that we can prevent.

Outpaced, not careless

A new secret appears in publicly visible code about once every two seconds, doubling yearly for the past three years. Public discourse is quick to jump to the idea that AI made developers careless.

Between Q2 2024 and Q2 2026, screened pushes grew 2.84 times while pushes carrying credentials grew 2.59 times. Across nine complete quarters of data, we found no statistically detectable trend regarding per-push prevalence. At the same time, we found data suggesting that, more than ever, developers understand the risk of accidental exposures and are less willing to accept that risk. Over the same period, the share of push-path blocks overridden by developers fell linearly from 6.63% to 3.93%. These figures challenge the common claim that agents are causing developers to become more careless.

More pushes, no clear rise in push prevalence

Public pushes, Q2 2024–Q2 2026. Push prevalence is the share with a detected secret. Covers supported provider patterns, including GitHub’s own tokens.

At a fixed rate, doubling activity doubles expected exposures. If each exposure requires the same human response, the workload doubles too. The mean time to manually revoke a secret hovers around 40 days; roughly one in five took more than 90 days. We’re accelerating the creation of software while exposed credentials can remain usable for weeks or months, because human remediation can’t scale at the same pace as development.

Telling developers to be more careful cannot, on its own, solve that problem. As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce human effort required by those that remain, if software development is to remain sustainable.

Prevention scales with compute

I’ve spent the past few years working on secret scanning at GitHub and the past year as product lead for the area. Our greatest impact has come from connecting the dots between detection and systems that can act.

GitHub’s catalog covers more than 150 technical partners through our secret scanning partnership program. Through our partner program, we work with participating secret issuers to build out detectors and report public exposures so they can respond. In Q2 2026, public scanning successfully reported an average of 26 credential matches a second, including repeat observations. Once notified, a large number of these partners immediately revoke the token: OpenAI API keys, Google Cloud account credentials, Slack webhooks, Hugging Face user tokens, SendGrid keys, etc. The owner may still need to replace the token, but revocation can happen without waiting for a developer to find and process a GitHub alert.

Push protection intervenes earlier. It stops recognizable credentials before they enter repository history, giving the developer or agent a chance to correct the change before there’s an exposure to investigate. We work with our technical partners to increase precision rates of their detectors as much as possible, until we’re confident enough to push-protect these secrets for the developer community by default.

Thanks to the efforts of our partners, in the past month, a secret was blocked by push protection at least once every second. When it comes to issuer-bound credentials, GitHub blocks more secrets than those which slip. I’m proud of how ordinary we’ve made that feel for developers.

Remediation scales with people

When including additional secret types, push protection stops about 30% of newly detected secrets before they enter repository history. We find the remaining 70% after the credential is, unfortunately, already lost. And:

  1. Prevention scales with compute, but remediation still scales with people.
  2. Refusing a push costs compute; cleaning up a secret already lost to visible history costs a developer’s time and attention.
  3. As the amount of code grows, we must prevent more exposures and reduce the human effort required by those that remain, or else the volume of vulnerabilities introduced will become untenable.

Telling developers to be more careful cannot solve this imbalance. Recognizing more of these secrets, earlier in development flows, is work the platform must take on.

Solving the four-body problem

Before a secret crosses the push boundary, the cost of stopping it is small, and the decision is binary: block or allow. After it crosses, the same string can authenticate to a real system, and the cost is unbounded.

In many cases, our only detection clue may be the surrounding code and world context. A provider-issued token may have a recognizable prefix. An internal database password may be completely unstructured, with no identifying pattern at all. We were already using context to find these secrets post-push; the problem was balancing that context-aware judgement with other factors.

We refer to this as the “four-body problem” for secret protection: precision, latency, throughput, and cost are coupled constraints. Prevention must be worth a developer’s time. A finding suitable for later review may not justify blocking a push. A false positive interrupts a developer and makes the next block harder to trust. A check that is too slow, expensive, or difficult to scale limits how often it can run.

Protection at the push in under 2 ms

Our new ModernBERT classifier assesses candidate secrets in context, without generating code or prose. It’s not only more precise than existing LLM-based pipelines, but it’s incredibly fast, evaluating candidate batches in under two milliseconds. It’s also extremely cost efficient, enough to run at scale in the critical path.

The inclusion of our model in push protection makes it possible for us to more than double the number of secrets that we’re able to prevent. The feature is currently in private preview. Later this month, the feature will be available to organizations with GitHub Secret Protection across Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Teams. It will consume AI credits.

We’re also bringing the model to developer surfaces beyond the push.

  • Starting today, any organization with AI secret detection will be automatically updated to the new model. Alerts opened from these post-push scans remain included with an organization’s purchase of secret scanning at no additional cost.
  • The model will also ship with GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23 in public preview, bringing AI-detected alerts to Secret Protection customers even in air-gapped environments.
  • We’re adding the classifier to the /security-review command for the Copilot CLI and Copilot App, so Copilot users can address secrets before a push even without needing an organization’s GitHub Secret Protection plan. AI credit usage will be attributed to GitHub Secret Protection in your AI usage insights.

Looking forward

The future we want is one where developers can entrust more work to agents without supervising every request, and one where the number of people that an organization needs to keep its credentials safe no longer scales with the amount of code it writes. We owe the developer community the same progress in protecting software that we are delivering in producing it.

We want people to build more software. Our capacity to protect it should grow with our capacity to create it.

The post Secret protection must scale with software appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

title: ReviewBench: An open benchmark for AI code review
feed_text:
Agentic code review is becoming an essential piece of how development happens. It helps you inspect pull requests, catch issues, and decide what deserves attention before code ships.

But the quality of existing AI reviewers can be hard to measure, and you need to know the strengths of a reviewer before you know if it will help you. Some reviewers surface more issues, some produce less noise, and some are stronger at catching critical problems while others surface smaller improvements, too. You may need code review to do different things within your workflow.

That makes it important to understand how reviewers actually compare: what different systems catch, what they miss, and the tradeoffs they make. A good code review benchmark should reflect the diversity of real pull requests, capture a broad set of review findings, and support meaningful breakdowns by severity, category, and precision-recall preferences. For teams building code review agents, the benchmark should also provide an offline signal that reliably tracks whether changes are likely to improve the experience in production. Existing benchmarks often make tradeoffs between label quality, coverage, and how well they represent real-world code review, leaving a gap for a rigorous and reproducible evaluation methodology that brings these pieces together.

We built ReviewBench, a new code review offline benchmark, to address that gap, and it is available for you to use today. It follows the language, repo size, and size distribution of pull requests, modeled after over 100 million real pull requests on GitHub. It uses a multi-source golden set and a consistent evaluation rubric and has been independently validated by senior engineers. Just as important, with the help of ReviewBench, our offline evaluation of Copilot code review (CCR) has become more effective at anticipating the direction of production experiments, giving us greater confidence that measured improvements reflect meaningful gains for users.

In this post, we’ll walk through how ReviewBench is constructed, how it establishes reliable ground truth and scoring, and how to onboard your own code review system and submit results.

Definitions of terms used in this blog post

  • Benchmark: A standardized evaluation that tests code reviewers on a common set of pull requests using the same scoring methodology.
  • Finding: A specific issue surfaced during code review.
  • Golden set: A validated collection of known findings for each pull request, used as a reference for evaluating what a reviewer catches or misses.
  • Precision: Of the issues a reviewer surfaces, the proportion that are valid. Higher precision generally means less noise.
  • Recall: Of the known valid issues, the proportion the reviewer finds. Higher recall means broader coverage.
  • F1 score: A single score that balances precision and recall equally.
  • Fβ score: A variation of F1 that lets you put more weight on either precision or recall, depending on your review preference.

ReviewBench at a glance

1

What we built

A realistic, comprehensive benchmark for AI code review agents

103.9M

GitHub pull requests

Analyze distributions by language, repository size, and change shape.

Representative benchmark corpus

219 public pull requests across 19 languages, aligned to GitHub-wide distributions while preserving substantive review cases.

Multi-source golden set

  • Human reviewers
  • Frontier LLMs
  • Static analysis

Structured findings

Every finding is labeled for severity and category, enabling user-tailored slices.

Severity

  • Critical
  • Medium
  • Low

Category

  • Correctness
  • Security
  • Reliability
  • Maintainability
  • Testing
  • ......

Evaluation metrics

Four metrics measure both known and newly discovered issues.

  • Grounded precision
  • Grounded recall
  • Augmented precision
  • Augmented recall

Objective evaluation

Measure improvement and compare across agents objectively. Help users choose the reviewer that fits their needs the best.

2

How we keep it trustworthy

An auditable chain from rubric to expert validation and production checks

Published rubric

One explicit standard for all findings.

Human-labeled dev set

Senior engineers establish ground truth.

Calibrated grader

Aligned with human judgment.

Uniform labeling

Same standard across all sources.

Published agreement

Expert audit of benchmark quality.

Auditable end to end

96.6% agreement

Senior engineers independently labeled golden true-positives before release.

Offline signals that anticipate production

Benchmark movement is checked against online experiments.

  • Improvements tend to show up online
  • Regressions tend to show up online too

How ReviewBench works

Our benchmark is built around five principles:

1. Representative pull requests, not a demo set

We analyzed 103.9 million GitHub pull requests to characterize the real-world distribution of code review workloads. ReviewBench contains 219 pull requests from 187 public open source licensed repositories spanning 19 languages, with its language and repository-size distributions closely matching GitHub overall. The complete benchmark dataset is publicly available.

We make one deliberate adjustment to this distribution: while language and repository size mirror GitHub directly, pull request size is weighted toward the reviewable middle and tail. This reduces the overrepresentation of tiny, single-file changes while preserving more substantive, multi-file pull requests where review quality matters most.

Quick corpus snapshot:

2. Broad ground truth discovery, independently judged

No single reviewer, whether human or model, can identify everything worth finding in a pull request. To build a broader and more reliable golden set for ground truth findings, we follow a three-stage process:

  • Gather candidate findings from diverse sources. We collect findings from real human reviewers, issues inferred from author follow-up commits, deterministic analysis tools, and multiple frontier LLMs across model families.
  • Semantically deduplicate overlapping findings. We merge findings that identify the same underlying issue, broadening coverage without allowing agreement across producers to artificially inflate the golden set or making it dependent on any one source’s blind spots.
  • Validate findings under a shared rubric. The source of a finding does not determine whether it is correct: a finding counts as a true positive only if it is true, relevant, and non-trivial. We use Claude Sonnet 5 as the LLM grader, applying a consistent evaluation rubric across all submissions. For transparency and reproducibility, we publish both the evaluation rubric and the judge used to apply it.

3. Metrics that measure both known and newly discovered issues

Most benchmarks report precision and recall against a fixed golden set. ReviewBench reports six metrics in two families:

  • Grounded precision, recall, and F1 score use only the existing gold-set labels. They provide the strict, apples-to-apples comparison: of the issues we already know about, how many did the agent find, and what share of its findings matched a known issue?
  • Augmented precision, recall and F1 score also evaluate findings that do not match anything in the golden set. The judge independently determines whether those unmatched findings are true or false positives, allowing a reviewer to receive credit for valid issues that no producer in the golden set surfaced

That distinction becomes more important as review agents become more capable. A fixed golden set inevitably becomes incomplete as systems discover issues its creators did not anticipate. Augmented metrics let ReviewBench recognize that behavior rather than automatically penalizing it. Because augmented recall expands the denominator based on what each agent discovers, we use grounded recall as the headline cross-system comparison and augmented metrics as an additional per-system diagnostic.

4. Configurable evaluation for different review preferences

There is no single universally optimal review experience. Some developers may want to focus only on critical issues, while others also value lower-severity, non-breaking findings. Some prefer broader coverage, while others prioritize precision and minimal noise. Others may have specialized needs, such as security- or privacy-focused review.

ReviewBench lets results be sliced by severity and category, while precision and recall capture different operating preferences. Users can also adjust β in the Fβ score to place more weight on recall for broader coverage or precision for lower noise. As these preferences change, the leaderboard is re-ranked accordingly, helping users identify the systems that best match their review priorities.

5. Internally audited and reproducibly evaluated

Before release, we asked senior engineers who had not participated in building the benchmark dataset to independently re-label every ground-truth finding from scratch. Their true/false-positive judgments agreed with ReviewBench 96.6% of the time. We version the benchmark dataset, judge, and matcher used in every evaluation, so results can be compared under the same benchmark configuration and revalidated when the benchmark changes. We also publish the validation methodology, agreement measurements, and known threats to validity, so readers can see how benchmark quality is assessed and where uncertainty remains.

Explore ReviewBench

ReviewBench’s research preview version is now available through the ReviewBench website, where you can explore the full benchmark, compare code review agents, and bring your own agent to evaluate and iterate.

With ReviewBench, you can:

  • Explore the full benchmark dataset. The complete ReviewBench dataset is publicly available, including the pull requests, findings, labels, severity and category annotations. This allows you to inspect exactly what systems are evaluated on and reproduce benchmark results.
  • Compare systems on the leaderboard. Results from evaluated code review agents using the full benchmark data are published on a common leaderboard, with views across overall performance, severity, category, and different precision–recall preferences.
  • Bring your own agent and hill-climb. The full benchmark dataset, evaluation methodology, LLM judge prompt, judge model configuration, and self-serve runner are publicly available, so you can evaluate your own code review agent, inspect its strengths and gaps, and iterate against the same benchmark configuration.

How we’ve used ReviewBench

We have used ReviewBench to evaluate Copilot code review (CCR) across successive iterations, giving us a consistent way to measure progress, catch regressions, and prioritize promising changes. Over time, this has helped us improve the product. One of the most valuable benefits of ReviewBench is that it provides an early offline signal of how a change to the product is likely to perform in production. Across experiments evaluated with ReviewBench before A/B testing, offline changes have consistently pointed in the same direction as what we see later in production.

A recent lite-tier experiment provides a concrete example of this broader pattern. We introduced a multi-model ensemble review that combines several independent model runs into a single review rather than relying on a single run. ReviewBench predicted higher precision, recall, and comment volume, along with lower cost per review.

To compare offline and production results, we use corresponding online signals. Addressed rate, our online counterpart to precision, is the percentage of CCR comments that an LLM determines prompted a developer to make a corresponding code change, based on the diff, thread, reactions, resolution state, and post-review code. For recall, we measure how much additional human review is still needed.

The online A/B test moved in the same direction as ReviewBench predicted: addressed rate (precision) rose 8.0%, recall rose 13.6%, and comment volume rose 61%, while cost per review fell 8.0%, all relative to the production control.

Comment volume alone, however, does not capture comment quality. More critical findings mean something very different from low-severity nits. ReviewBench’s severity-level evaluation captured this too: it predicted a 227% increase in critical comments, compared with 262% online, along with the same broader shift toward more moderate comments and fewer nits.

This gives us a fast and repeatable signal before running production experiments. Online experiments remain the ultimate measure of user impact, but ReviewBench gives us greater confidence in which changes are worth taking there.

How to submit your own run

  1. Sign in with GitHub on the ReviewBench website.
  2. Register your agent. Provide a container image, your configuration, and your own model key. We provide the judge.
  3. Try it on the test set. Run against a 25-PR test set with per-PR detail and repeat as you tune your configuration.
  4. Do a final run. When you’re ready, run the full set of 219 pull requests (three rounds), scored by the same judge as every other entry.
  5. Publish to the leaderboard. Your scores remain private until a maintainer reviews and approves the submission. Scores are published to the leaderboard only if they outperform the agent’s current leaderboard score, or if this is the agent’s first leaderboard entry.

We invite you to explore ReviewBench, evaluate your own system, challenge our assumptions, and help us improve the benchmark. We’re excited to collaborate with researchers and practitioners to make code review evaluation more open, reliable, and useful—and ultimately help move AI code review forward.

Acknowledgments

ReviewBench was a team effort across GitHub and Microsoft. We’re grateful to the researchers and engineers who built it: those who designed the methodology, curated the pull requests, built the golden set and the evaluation pipeline, and made the benchmark something anyone can run.

The post ReviewBench: An open benchmark for AI code review appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

title: AI is changing developer work. Here are three skills to strengthen.
feed_text:
AI is changing how developers work and apply their skills. Writing code is still essential, but developers increasingly need to know how to direct AI, evaluate its output, communicate tradeoffs, and make sound technical decisions.

The good news? You can start preparing today. Here’s where to focus:

Tip #1: Learn to direct AI, not just use it.

AI is changing what execution looks like. Increasingly, great execution means defining the problem clearly, providing the right context, evaluating AI-generated code, and deciding what’s ready to ship. As AI agents take on more of the implementation, these skills become even more valuable.

For example, imagine you’re asked to add a new authentication flow.

A traditional workflow might look like this:

Task: Add authentication  

→ Create branch  
→ Write code  
→ Run tests  
→ Open pull request

As AI tools become more capable and more deeply integrated into day-to-day workflows, those same skills can help you coordinate multiple AI agents. Your workflow might look more like this:

Workspace: Add authentication  

Agent 1 ✓ Authentication ready for review 
Agent 2 ✓ Documentation draft ready  
Agent 3 ✓ Test suite ready

Notice what changed. You’re still responsible for the outcome, but you’re spending less time implementing every piece yourself. Instead, you’re defining the work, reviewing outputs, and making the technical decisions that bring everything together.

Takeaway: Learn to direct AI agents.

Start your first agent session >

Tip #2: Don’t trust AI’s first answer

AI can generate impressive solutions in seconds, but the first answer isn’t always the best. Your experience writing clean, maintainable code can help you evaluate AI’s output.

Ask a second AI model to critique the first model’s work, then use your own judgment to evaluate both responses.

Here’s a prompt that shows what that might look like in practice:

"Write a SQL query that returns each customer's most recent order." 
↓ 
AI Model #1 
✓ Generates the query 
↓ 
AI Model #2 (Critique) 
⚠ Doesn't handle duplicate timestamps 
⚠ Missing index recommendation 
⚠ May perform poorly on large tables

Different AI models have different strengths and blind spots. That’s why GitHub Copilot’s built-in Rubber Duck agent uses a second model to critique plans, code, and tests before you move forward. A second perspective often catches issues the first model misses.

Takeaway: Trust AI enough to use it but not enough to skip review.

Tip #3: Use AI to solve bigger problems

When AI saves implementation time, developers can use that time to tackle broader problems: understanding customer needs, evaluating tradeoffs, designing better systems, and making technical decisions that AI can’t make for them.

For example:

Issue #4821 
Title: Add dark mode 

AI 

✓ Build implementation 
✓ Generate tests 
✓ Update documentation 

Developer checklist 

☐ Validate customer problem 
☐ Review architectural tradeoffs 
☐ Check accessibility 
☐ Define success metrics 
☐ Approve solution

As AI takes on more implementation work, the skills that distinguish great engineers become even more important: exercising sound judgment, balancing tradeoffs, and solving the right problems.

Takeaway: Let AI handle more of the implementation so you can spend more time building the judgment that helps teams make better decisions.

The bottom line

As developer workflows evolve, learning to work effectively with AI—and strengthening your own technical judgment—can help you adapt.

Put these ideas in practice >

title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to build custom workflows with canvases
feed_text:
Most tools give you a fixed set of screens and ask you to fit your work into them. But what if you could start with the workflow you want instead and have the interface take shape around it?

That’s the idea behind canvases in the GitHub Copilot app. A canvas, also called a canvas extension, is a customizable interface that you and the agent share. It can be a kanban board, an issue triage board, a release checklist, a dashboard, a form, or even a spreadsheet: a UI shaped to how you work.

Because the canvas is bidirectional, the agent can update it as it works, and you can use buttons, cards, filters, and other controls to make changes too. Just like using a live shared whiteboard.

Let’s create one.

Creating a canvas with /create-canvas

To create a canvas, you don’t have to do any coding or design by hand. Just open an agent session, enter the /create-canvas skill, and describe what you want in plain English.

Make sure your prompt covers three things:

  • The workflow the canvas should support.
  • What you should be able to do in the interface.
  • What the agent should be able to do.

For example, you could enter:

/create-canvas Create a release notes canvas for tracking new feature work completed across GitHub Copilot app sessions. Include controls for reviewing and organizing entries and allow the agent to add and update them.

Then, the agent will build the interface and open it in the right-side panel without you having to write files or mess with the layout. One description becomes a custom tool that’s ready to use.

Shaping the canvas around your workflow

Because the interface is generated from your description, your first version is just a starting point, and you can keep refining until you’re happy.

You could ask the agent to add a column or filter, pull in your open pull requests, or turn the entire canvas into a checklist for your day. The agent will revise the canvas to match. While there isn’t a fixed menu of layouts, if you can describe a workflow, you can likely turn it into a canvas.

Once created, your canvas is saved as an extension, so you can use it again. You can keep it with the project for your team to share or save it as a personal extension just for you.

Instant collaboration, not command and wait

The real power of a canvas is that you and the agent can both keep working at the same time.

When you click a button, update a field, or move a card, the canvas’ shared state changes immediately. The agent sees the same update without a separate send or sync step.

It works the other way, too. You can ask the agent to use the canvas’ own capabilities—the same actions available to you—to add a release note or move a card, then watch that change appear in the interface. Instead of sending a command and waiting for a response, you’re steering the work together.

Take this with you

Creating a useful canvas starts with three simple questions:

  • What information do I want to see?
  • What do I want to change directly?
  • What should the agent be able to update or do?

Not sure where to begin? The community has shared ready-made canvas extensions through Awesome Copilot, including release notes tools, kanban boards, issue triage workflows, and more. Install one that’s close to what you need, then ask the agent to customize it for your workflow in the same way you would refine a canvas you created yourself.

Start small: open a session, run /create-canvas, and describe a simple board or checklist for something you’re working on now.

Try using the GitHub Copilot app >
