title: Building resilient AI-powered software, and planning for when things go wrong
feed_text:
Last week’s guest on the podcast was Sam Newman, who had released a book I’ve personally long awaited titled Building Resilient Distributed Systems. It’s an especially timely book for many of us software engineers, as we’re seeing more outages with nearly all services and systems – much of it caused by more code deploys thanks to AI agents writing more code; and more bugs causing more incidents in production.

Sam’s book being “fresh out of the oven,” it naturally also touches on what AI changes as we design resilient systems. In fact, Sam told me that he took a total of three years to finishe the book – instead of the two he originally planned – because he went back and reworked all parts of the book, updating parts where AI is relevant to talk about.

I asked Sam if he would consider sharing an excerpt from the book, with sections especially relevant for anyone building systems that ought to be reliable. Sam graciously agreed, and today’s issue covers a few important topics, spread across two chapters from his book. We get into:

  1. Disaster recovery (DR). Recovering from catastrophic failures: planning for cloud region/data center/site-wide outages, the concept of RPO and RTO, DRO objectives and SLOs.

  2. Disaster Recovery Patterns. Backup-and-restore, pilot light failover, warm failover and multisite active-active.

  3. Infrastructure availability when planning for DR. Ongoing GPU and CPU shortages mean you cannot expect infrastructure availability at all times, so you need to understand constraints your vendors have, and to prioritize critical services.

  4. Resiliency of AI-powered software. Model provider resilience, the challenge of models changing, and the need for observability.

  5. How to handle uncertainty. Tactics like being multi-model and multi-vendor, making costs transparent, and frequently analyzing vendors.

Even though this article is pretty long, we cover less than a full chapter from the book's 16 chapters. If you build reliable systems for a living, I warmly recommend the book itself, and you can get it from the publisher.

My usual disclaimer: as with all my recommendations, I was not paid to recommend this book, and none of the links are affiliate ones. See my ethics statement for more details.

The excerpts below are from Building Resilient Distributed Systems, by Sam Newman. Copyright © 2026 Sam Newman. Published by O’Reilly Media, Inc. Used with permission.

1. Disaster Recovery

Excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery.

We’ve already discussed how to handle a variety of failures that impact individual service instances. But what happens when a catastrophic failure causes widespread outage of large parts of your system? Fire, flood, electrical supply issues, and errors in the underlying cloud infrastructure are all outside of your control, and at one fell swoop, they can render your attempts to make your system more robust totally redundant.

Handling these situations falls under the auspices of disaster recovery (DR), a set of procedures that should kick in when something really bad happens. As with much of what we’ve looked at in this book, trade-offs abound. As you reduce your period of acceptable downtime or data loss, cost and complexity increase, so picking the right approach for your system can be a delicate balancing act. In this chapter, I’ll give you some concrete targets to work with to help drive your own DR approach.

Cloud Region, Data Center, or Site?

The exact terminology you use to discuss your infrastructure will likely vary based on implementation details, and this in turn can make discussions around generally applicable patterns more difficult. When running on the public cloud, for example, you’ll probably be familiar with the concept of a cloud region, which is where your cloud resources live. When running on a private cloud or in a more traditional on-premises setup, you’ll instead think in terms of data centers.

As we discuss the various options around handling DR, the patterns that we’ll see later in this chapter can be used for either public or private cloud scenarios. Therefore, to keep things simple, I’ll use the term site as a general descriptor of where your computing infrastructure lives.

There are some specific issues to consider around mixing cloud vendors as part of a DR strategy, and we’ll look more at those in Chapter 11.

How Good Does Your DR Need to Be?

A spectrum of DR options are available to you, and they can range greatly in terms of cost, complexity, and recovery. To help you decide which DR approach is most appropriate, we should first try to understand how to determine the appropriate requirements for your context.

A simple way to define technical requirements around DR is to make use of two concrete measurable targets, recovery point objective and recovery time objective. In Figure 10-1, you can see how these objectives relate to an incident:

Recovery Point Objective

The recovery point objective (RPO) defines the maximum amount of time that can have passed since the data was last backed up or synchronized. Put another way, RPO defines the upper duration of potential data loss. If the data for your system backs up once an hour, then it’s possible to lose up to an hour of data if your system has an incident. Therefore, your RPO would be an hour.

Recovery Time Objective

The recovery time objective (RTO) defines how long it’s acceptable for your system to be unavailable in the wake of an incident. If all your computers became unavailable, perhaps because of a data center–wide outage, how long would it take you to have your services running in an alternative data center? Your RTO includes all the time needed to recover data from the last recovery point, make computing resources available for your workloads, and redirect traffic to your new site—so there are more variables to consider in terms of bringing your system back online than just time.

You Can’t Have Everything

If asked what RPO and RTO you’d want in a vacuum, you’d probably give a very simple answer: you’d want an RPO of zero (i.e., a guarantee of no data loss), and an RTO of zero too. This is an understandable wish, but as you reduce your RPO and RTO, cost and complexity increase dramatically—and in technical terms, it’s not possible to guarantee a zero RPO or RTO in any case.

An additional complication is that different types of workloads might require different RPOs and RTOs. Consider a bank, for example. Having a low RPO to ensure that payment information isn’t lost would be key, and having a low RTO to ensure that people can still take money out of their account is vital. On the other hand, the part of the system that enables new customers to sign up for an account could have a higher RTO and RPO, as the impact to the business is less severe.

So when deciding on the appropriate RPO and RTO, there needs to be a discussion with stakeholders regarding end-user needs and regulatory and legislative requirements, which are balanced against the cost and complexity of implementing the required solution. For example, your product owner might initially say they need an RPO of 10 minutes, but if you could tell them it would take months of work to implement (during which other work has to be deprioritized), they might reduce their target, perhaps accepting an RPO that is easier for you to deliver. Your target RPO and RTO should also exceed anything specified in any service level agreements you have.

DR Objectives and SLOs

At first glance, RPO and RTO would appear to make for good service level objectives (SLOs). After all, they are both important measures that directly impact user experience. However, there are some challenges around managing RPO and RTO as SLOs.

When determining if we are meeting an SLO, we need to collect lots of service level indicators (SLI) to confirm whether or not we are on target. So if we had an SLO that defined 99th percentile latency over a one-month period of less than 500 milliseconds, we would analyze the latency-related SLIs for that monthlong period to make sure we were meeting the target. With RPO and RTO, though, what would our SLI be?

The reality is that we don’t experience disasters regularly enough to gather useful SLIs. We can of course define related SLOs around things related to our DR approach. For example, it would be possible to define an SLO around the speed of data replication, as this is something we are doing in production and can programmatically measure. But at best SLOs are only tangentially measuring RPO and RTO.

So RPOs and RTOs don’t really fit neatly into the SLO concept. Of course, that doesn’t mean that you can’t still test your system to make sure it is delivering on your DR objectives—something we’ll discuss more later in the chapter.

4. Disaster Recovery Patterns

Another excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery.

With the discussion of RPO and RTO in mind, let’s take a look at some common patterns used to implement DR in the wake of a major incident. In Figure 10-2, we can see an overview of each of the four patterns we will explore, arranged (broadly speaking) in order of increasing complexity and improving RTO and RPO.

If starting from scratch, many of these patterns can build on one another, allowing you to incrementally increase the complexity (and cost) of your DR solution over time. For example, a backup and restore approach requires rerouting, a pilot light setup will add the need for cross-site data replication and infrastructure automation, and a warm failover adds on the cost of having some infrastructure ready to go. So if you aren’t sure where to start, working your way through the patterns from left to right in Figure 10-2 makes a lot of sense.

If you have different RPO and RTOs for different parts of your system, you may also end up using a mix of these patterns. Note that they all require some form of rerouting of traffic, and most require some form of cross-site data replication. Those options are discussed later in this chapter.

Pattern: Backup and Restore

Recovery by restoring data from a backup and loading it into a replacement system.

As outlined in Figure 10-3, with this pattern, data is periodically backed up to a separate site. In the event that the primary site fails, infrastructure needs to be provided at a new site, and the backed-up data restored.

How it works

This pattern is very straightforward to implement, consisting of a few steps:

1. Back up data regularly.

All data that you want to make available to the failover site needs to be regularly backed up, with the backup data stored somewhere other than the primary site.

2. Provision infrastructure on the failover site.

This would ideally be automated, as manual infrastructure provisioning would likely lead to longer RTO and an increased chance of errors.

3. Restore data from backup to the failover site.

Data is loaded from the backup location into the newly provisioned infrastructure.

4. Switch traffic from the primary to the failover site.

Once infrastructure is available and the data is restored, traffic can be switched to the secondary.

Ideally, your failover site runs the same core technology stack as the primary site, meaning that any investment in infrastructure automation on your primary can also be used on the failover (for example, being able to reuse Terraform scripts). Keeping the code to automate setup of the primary and the failover the same is very useful, as it means that you’ll have a higher degree of confidence that spinning up the infrastructure on the failover site will work. If your failover site uses a different technology stack—meaning it’s not possible to share automated infrastructure provisioning code between the primary and secondary sites—then it becomes even more vital that your DR failover process is regularly tested. A caveat to spinning up infrastructure on demand here comes in terms of guaranteeing that infrastructure is actually available when you need it, something we’ll explore later in this chapter.

When to use it

This pattern is generally applicable in situations where your primary site is unavailable and you can tolerate a long RTO, and especially in those situations where you want to keep costs low. It’s important to note that regular tests of a backup and restore process are necessary to ensure that it actually works. One approach I’ve found useful is to perform a backup and restore to a secondary site as part of other regular activity (for example, a regular load test exercise).

The RPO of this pattern will depend on the frequency of backup. The RTO will be the longest of the patterns we’ll look at, and its time will depend primarily on how long it takes to restore data from the backup and provision replacement resources. With a fully automated process and smaller data volumes, this could be in the minutes to hours range. Manual recovery processes will likely extend these timelines greatly, as will the size of backups involved—terabytes of data take longer to send than gigabytes! Another major factor will be availability of the required computing resources. If you end up having to purchase replacement equipment, this pattern could easily result in a timeline of weeks or longer.

Pattern: Pilot Light Failover

Data is constantly synced to a failover site, with infrastructure provisioned after failover.

With a pilot light setup, data is continually replicated from the primary to the failover site, as shown in Figure 10-4. Infrastructure is not provisioned until a failover is required, ensuring that costs can be kept down when working with public cloud infrastructure.

How it works

This pattern builds on a lot of the work done with a backup and restore, the main change being that the data is continually synchronized to the failover site. As such, the steps involved look fairly similar to the backup and restore pattern:

1. Replicate data continually.

As data is committed to the primary, it is continually replicated to the failover site. This can be done in a variety of ways, such as by making use of native database technology or application-level replication.

2. Provision infrastructure on the failover site.

The assumption is that databases and datastores are already present on the failover site, so only remaining resources like compute would need to be provisioned.

3. Switch traffic from the primary to the failover site.

Once infrastructure is available and the data is restored, traffic can be switched to the failover.

From an implementation point of view, the new source of complexity comes from the replication of data from the primary to the failover. For systems designed with this process in mind, it might be somewhat trivial to implement. However, things become more complex when adapting existing systems if you’re making use of a data product that doesn’t support this replication strategy natively. This is worthy of a more in-depth discussion later in this chapter, especially as the next two patterns also rely on this capability.

When to use it

When compared to a backup and restore, the pilot light failover allows for a much shorter RPO because of more frequent data replication, while also reducing RTO by eliminating the time taken for data restoration.

The cost-saving of a pilot light failover really makes sense only in the context of the public cloud. Costs are reduced primarily in terms of not paying for infrastructure unless it’s used. But if your failover site is your own private infrastructure that you have to pay for regardless of whether it is used, then some form of a warm failover makes a lot more sense. At that point you’re already paying for the hardware, so you might as well use it.

Pattern: Warm Failover

Data is synced to a failover site, with at least some infrastructure already provisioned to handle traffic.

With a warm failover, as shown in Figure 10-5, data is continually replicated from the primary to the failover site, with at least some infrastructure already provisioned in advance of the failover itself.

Having some infrastructure provisioned even before the failover occurs results in a reduction in RTO for some functionality. How much infrastructure is provisioned on the failover can vary, but the idea is that some capacity already exists to allow for a much faster failover.

A common approach would be to prioritize the subset infrastructure that is provided on the secondary site for the more critical capabilities of the system, allowing for a shorter RTO for the most important functionality.

Cold, Warm, and Hot Failovers: A brief note is warranted here regarding the term warm. You’ll find various solutions and vendor products promising cold, warm, or hot failover, with the only real distinguishing factor between these terms often being that a hot failover would give you a lower RTO in comparison to a warm failover, and a warm failover would give you a lower RTO than a cold one. Given that what constitutes hot or warm from vendor to vendor and from tech stack to tech stack varies so greatly, I just decided to pick warm and stick with it.

Naming things is hard.

The “How it works” and “When to use it sections” are cut off from this excerpt, but are present inside the book.

Pattern: Multisite Active-Active

The system is distributed across two or more sites, with writes being able to be sent to any site.

With a multisite active-active setup, data is replicated constantly between two or more sites, as you can see in Figure 10-6. Traffic for any customer can be served from any site at any time.

This pattern sidesteps the need for a failover, as it is assumed that traffic for any user can switch between sites at any time. As such, it delivers the lowest RTO and RPO of any pattern we’ve looked at so far, though at much higher cost and complexity.

The “How it works” and “When to use it sections” are cut off from this excerpt, but are present inside the book.

3. Infrastructure availability when planning for DR

Yet another excerpt from Chapter 10: Disaster Recovery.

At the time of writing, GenAI is being used by more and more industries. Whatever your views on the usefulness of this technology (or its broader societal impact), the nature of GenAI workloads for both training and inference purposes has driven ever-increasing demand for infrastructure, in turn leading to reduced capacity for many users. Even if you aren’t running what you consider to be specialized GenAI workloads (for example, those requiring specific GPUs), you may well see the impact of these shortages more broadly.

Aside from the ever-growing cost of GPUs, memory costs have spiked significantly in 2025 and 2026, impacting general server availability. I’ve already spoken to clients who are struggling to run “normal” (non-AI) workloads on some of the large public cloud providers, as they can’t secure enough capacity. Being able to shift regions in some cases is helping, but guarantees of future availability seem fairly weak. Even buying your own hardware doesn’t seem to be a quick fix, with lead times for servers seemingly extending further and further with each passing week.

This has to be taken into account when considering the patterns detailed previously. If your chosen approach assumes you can dynamically provision infrastructure when a failure occurs, you will have to look at what guarantees you have around the capacity you want. In a scenario where a major cloud vendor’s region has failed, you may find yourself fighting over scraps with everyone else.

There are three ways to handle this scenario: reserve capacity; prioritize critical services; or lastly, consider running a fully redundant set of infrastructure at all times.

Not every vendor offers the ability to reserve capacity, and even then it is limited to certain cloud services. On AWS, for example, you can pay a fee to guarantee the availability of EC2 instances (managed virtual machines) when you need them. This has a cost impact, as you pay a fee for the reservation whether or not you use the instances (the silver lining being that if you did end up using them, the cost would be cheaper than normal in-demand pricing). This doesn’t help you, though, when using cloud resources for which reservations aren’t possible—you can’t purchase guaranteed availability of Lambda invocations, for example.

Next, consider prioritizing critical services. If there is a cost to guaranteeing availability (or if only a limited amount of infrastructure is available), then it’s vital that this goes to workloads that have a higher criticality. This is where having separate RTOs and RPOs on a service-by-service basis comes into play.

Finally, if you could justify the complexity and expense of having a fully redundant set of infrastructure ready to run your system, then you’d have the confidence that your computing resources will be available, with the caveat that this option can be extremely costly. But that cost can be mitigated if you can make alternative use of the redundant resources.

Back in Chapter 4, I mentioned BankCo, where we ran calculations across a large pool of machines. A large portion of these computers were desktop PCs sitting idle in an office situated outside London. These PCs formed part of the bank’s DR strategy: in the event that traders had to evacuate the bank’s main location, they could relocate to the secondary site and continue working. It was a requirement that these standby PCs were constantly running to ensure that we knew that they worked, and so that updates could be pushed out to them. This was obviously back in the day when most of the critical work relied on thick-client applications, so they couldn’t be accessed via the web.

We were able to make use of these DR workstations to grow our pool of available workers. This meant that when the DR site wasn’t in operation (which was most of the time), we were able to carry out our calculations much faster, as we could parallelize the work over more machines. If the DR site’s machines were unavailable to us, we still had a set of our own servers on which we could run the calculations to suit our normal targets.

So if you are thinking about securing ring-fenced infrastructure as part of a DR approach, see if you can think of useful ways to put it to good use when it’s not needed for production workloads. You could use the spare infrastructure for a load test environment, for example; the load test could easily be aborted when DR is needed.

4. Resiliency of AI-powered software

Excerpt from Chapter 7: Resiliency and AI

We’ve looked at how AI is changing how we build and operate our software. But we are also integrating AI into the products we build, using it to hopefully improve our software for our users. What new challenges does this create for ensuring our systems are resilient?

Model Provider Resiliency

Foundation model providers OpenAI and Anthropic don’t have a great track record in terms of providing high levels of availability for their services, at least when compared to other managed service providers, like public cloud vendors. While I’m sure this will improve over time, having a potentially flaky third party in the mix of your critical functionality can be an issue.

A solution here is to consider ensuring that your software can still operate even if the model is unavailable. This could be achieved by limiting functionality in the case of the model being unavailable (or you getting rate limited or running out of tokens!)—this is an example of the graceful degradation pattern, which we’ll look at more in Chapter 11.

Another option is to have backup vendors for a given model to hedge against your normal model provider having availability issues. For example, you can use OpenAI models on Azure, a handy alternative if accessing the models via OpenAI’s own services proves to be too unstable, and in a similar way Anthropic’s models can also be accessed via Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. When using backup vendors like this, there may be a lag in terms of how quickly the latest models may be available, but given that you may not always want to be on the bleeding edge of the models you use to embed in your software (something we’ll discuss in just a moment), this is probably fine.

Model Changes

Consistency of behavior plays a big role in helping us ensure that our system is behaving appropriately. While dealing with the unexpected is a key concept in resiliency (or “graceful extensibility,” as David Woods put it), that doesn’t mean we want to build software where surprise is constant. Quite aside from the fact that LLMs are nondeterministic, small changes in models can also lead to quite different behavior.

I’ve seen reports where a model has started behaving differently, without any major change in behavior being flagged by the vendor. Additionally, moving to a newer version of a model can fundamentally change how your prompts may be handled.

It is therefore vital to have a good set of tests to validate that the AI portions of your code are behaving appropriately—and this should be a mix of traditional functional tests, together with the use of AI evaluation tools (evals). You want to make sure that when the unexpected occurs, you are ones who get surprised first, rather than your users.

I can recommend the second edition of Gayathri Mohan’s Full Stack Testing,3 for those of you wanting to explore testing in general, including verification of AI-based systems. For a deeper dive specifically into evals, I’d suggest Evals for AI Engineers by Shreya Shankar and Hamel Husain.

Observability

The telemetry we receive from our own software and from third-party services alike is key to making sure our applications are working the way that we expect. As we discussed back in Chapter 3, we prefer a small variation of latency rather than a broad variation of latency. If the time it takes to successfully complete an operation varies wildly, it can be difficult to know where we should start triggering timeouts, for example. It also becomes more difficult to define latency-related SLOs.

Once you send a prompt to an AI model or instruct an agent to do something for you, the latency for the operation can vary greatly, and in ways that can be difficult to predict from the outset. Some of this can be put down to variability in the performance of the provider at a given point in time, but it can also be the result of rate limiting by the provider, or your prompt could just be taking longer to process.

In situations where the prompts sent to models come directly from your users, then you will likely have even less certainty about how long it should take for a model to come back to you. Has a call hung, or is it expecting a large output?

Some techniques to solve this can include dynamically setting timeouts based on the number of tokens being generated, or monitoring the streaming output from a model so you can track when the response starts coming back rather than waiting for the full response.

5. How to handle uncertainty

Excerpt from Chapter 7: Resiliency and AI

In the previous sections, I’ve outlined why the world of AI is so uncertain right now. However, I want this book to focus on practical, actionable advice. With that in mind, I want to outline some key steps you can take to make sure that you’re prepared for the uncertainty ahead.

Multimodel, Multivendor

With model behavior, speed, and quality changing from version to version, it’s vital that you build your software to support changing models. Not only do you want the ability to change models to make use of the latest and greatest, but if costs start to increase from one vendor, you want to make sure the barrier to finding another vendor isn’t too great.

It is worth highlighting that mixing models from different vendors in a single flow can exacerbate issues. For example, a flow that involved models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google’s Gemini would be impacted if any of those models had availability issues. All those models have to be available and functioning correctly at the time the flow is executed. Also, prompts that work against one model may not be entirely portable to another—a prompt tuned against one model will have to be reevaluated when moving to a different model, even if you stay within the same vendor ecosystem.

Taking a multimodel approach extends to your vendors too. If a vendor you are dependent on is in turn dependent on a single vendor’s model or API, you and your vendor become vulnerable to volatility in that model or to being impacted by a sudden price increase. Cursor was forced to pass on a significant cost increase to its customers in 2025, as it relied on the use of Anthropic’s services, and Anthropic changed its pricing structure, which led to Cursor having to pay much more. Coincidentally, Anthropic’s Claude Code is a direct competitor of Cursor. If Cursor had been able to use AI models from another firm, it might have been less vulnerable to this issue.

Keep Your Options Open: Make sure you aren’t wholly dependent on a single model or AI platform. If model quality degrades, or prices from OpenAI or Anthropic go up, you want to make sure that you have the flexibility to go elsewhere.

Cost Transparency

Given concerns about rising costs from vendors, and given that pay-as-you-go pricing models can lead to surprising and unsustainable bills, having the ability to see on a regular basis how much money you are spending, and where, can be really important. This doesn’t need to be about limiting spend necessarily; it can be about understanding how you spend money and understanding what value that brings.

James Stanier, CTO at digital healthcare firm Nordhealth, has advocated for being able to see spend on a per-person basis. Rather than this being about shaming people who spend too much money, he makes the case that this visibility drives better understanding of how the software is being used and helps drive the adoption of tools that are proving to be valuable. In his 2025 talk at LeadDev Berlin, “LLMs: An Operator’s View”, Stanier explains that if you see a person spending a lot of money, this shouldn’t be seen as a bad thing, as typically it showsomeone trying to get more done. He cites an example of one of his QA engineers blowing through €1,000 in a single week on Claude Code, which was a much higher spend than normal. After pairing with the engineer in question to understand where this money was going, Stanier was able to see that this spend allowed the engineer in question to more than double his productivity.

Having the information about spend available to you, and being able to talk to people about how they use these tools and the benefits (or problems) they cause, will help you all make much better and more informed decisions.

It can also help you spot egregious overspend. Uber recently revealed that it had burned through its entire annual AI budget in just the first four months of the year, and Microsoft announced it was pulling Claude licenses from its employees, due in part to cost, apparently.5 These stories might cause one or two raised eyebrows, but they pale in comparison to the recent (admittedly unsubstantiated) report from Axios that an unnamed enterprise company spent $500 million on Claude licenses after failing to put cost controls into place.

Tip: Make your AI spend visible! It can help you understand how people are using it and also help you spot when the bills start climbing precipitously.

More Frequent Vendor Analysis

Vendor management is a common activity that many firms carry out. It typically consists of a regular review of the main vendors that the organization makes use of to help it make better decisions in the future. For example, seeing that a large amount of money is being spent with a particular vendor despite the quality of service from said vendor degrading might cause an escalation to either get the price reduced or get the quality of service improved—or it might kick off a process to find a replacement.

In my last role at Thoughtworks, I helped lead our internal technology operations. Although my main job was to help provide support to internal delivery teams, I was also involved from time to time with our own vendor management activities. As part of these activities, we would regularly assess the general health of the vendors themselves. During the last review I was involved with, we were actively concerned about the health of one of our main technology suppliers; the supplier was in a very competitive market, and its market share was dropping. Although we were happy with the quality of service it provided (and with the cost), our fear was that wider market forces would drive it out of business. As a result, we decided to get to know the vendor much better but to also prepare a list of alternative solutions that we could select if the vendor in question didn’t survive.

Given the degree of uncertainty around the AI sector in general, I’d recommend regular vendor management activities. If you already have a normal vendor analysis cycle, consider increasing its frequency for AI vendors. If possible, find out if any vendors are in turn dependent on another provider, as in the case of Cursor being dependent on Anthropic’s cloud services. I’d be more concerned about a vendor that is in turn wholly dependent on a single company than I would be about a vendor that has more flexibility about whose services it uses. If you’ve never done vendor management before, consider instituting a lightweight process so you can build up a better understanding of how exposed you are to risk in this space.

With the concerns around the potential security vulnerabilities that come from the use of AI, I’d also recommend keeping your threat model up-to-date with regular threat assessments. As with vendor reviews, consider increasing the frequency of your normal threat assessments in areas with heavy use of AI, as this technology and how we use it is changing very quickly.

Review Your AI Vendors Regularly! Given the volatility in the space, make sure you review your AI vendors much more frequently than normal vendors.

Summary

I realize that this chapter may have ended on somewhat of a negative note. But I wanted to be clear that we have real, practical use cases for AI in helping us build more resilient distributed systems. Most of the use cases I outlined in this chapter are being used daily by people all over the world. The key thing is that the solutions I have shared here still put humans at the heart of decision making. It’s clear that, due to the challenges I have covered here as well, we are a long way from a truly autonomous AI SRE.

Despite the obvious benefits of using AI, we do need to be fully aware of the downsides at both the micro and macro level. At the micro level, LLM-powered AI requires us to be OK with nondeterminism, whereas there are many activities we perform in the context of building resilient systems that need to be fully repeatable and deterministic. At the macro level, concerns about the AI sector as a whole mean we are dealing with an ever-changing (and hopefully) improving set of products built on very shaky financial foundations. It doesn’t matter how good the tooling is if it’s too expensive to use (or the company making it goes bust).

As is the nature of things, this uncertainty around AI’s role in our industry and society as a whole will fade as we learn more and as the market settles down. But be warned: I think we are still very much in the middle of the storm, and the calm waters may be several years away yet.

A lot of this chapter was about uncertainty, and one thing that can make the resiliency of a system quite uncertain is what happens when machines fail. So in Chapter 8, I’ll explore how to make sure our systems still work even when machines let us down.

Takeaways

Gergely, again.

Thanks to Sam for sharing this excerpt of the book! While this was a long article in itself, we covered less than one of 16 chapters in the book. I found the book an excellent read, and recommend getting it if you’re building production systems:

Get the ebook or print book

My sense is that AI is making “resiliency basics” more important than before. Most of the book is not about AI – in fact, AI is barely mentioned in many of the chapters. But as AI agents generate more code and allow building software faster than before: we now have more software (or more complex software!) to operate.

And while there are AI tools and vendors that promise operating software to be easier with AI: I don’t really buy that it is, at least not at scale. Having the right monitoring and alerting in place is becoming more important, as is responding to outages, and being aware of tricky situations like thundering herds, retries, idempotency, timeouts, and many others.

Preparing for disaster recovery seems like a practical thing to do when your service is important enough. I wanted to include excerpts on disaster recovery, because I observe plenty of “disasters” (that is, widespread outages) happening across the industry where recovery time becomes surprisingly long. And some of this could be because the team had not prepared for, or exercised, disaster recovery beforehand.

A good example is how Coinbase’s global trading service went offline after a single AWS zone had problems. As I summarized the incident in The Pulse, back in June:

“Having no automated failovers is incredibly amateurish for an operation of Coinbase’s scale. Coinbase moves about 5.2 trillion dollars per year, and is valued at around $40B. The outage interrupted around $7 billion-worth of financial activity, based on my napkin math.”

It’s smart to learn from the mistakes of others, when we can: and the Coinbase incident felt like one of these.

I hope you found these topics relevant, and thanks again to Sam for writing the book, and sharing relevant parts with us.

title: Building resilient systems with Sam Newman
feed_text:
Stream the latest episode

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

In this episode

Sam Newman wrote one of the most-read books about microservices (“Building Microservices”), but he calls them an architecture of “last resort.”

In this episode of the Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Sam explains his thinking on this, and he’s certainly well placed to do so; he was in the room when the term “microservices” was coined. We discuss what teams get wrong when adopting microservices, why independent deployment matters, and how microservices can help teams work more autonomously.

We also peek into his new book, ‘Building Resilient Distributed Systems’, and Sam explains his three rules for distributed systems, why observability is essential, and also why it’s vital to take business context into account when deciding whether to fail open or fail closed on errors.

We also explore how AI is changing software development, from specs versus code as a source of truth to cognitive debt and cognitive surrender. Sam shares how modular architecture can help teams experiment with AI while maintaining understanding of the systems being built.

Takeaways from the conversation with Sam

1. In the room when “microservices” was coined. In the early years of the 2010s, James Lewis – Sam’s colleague at Thoughtworks – kept running into companies building service-oriented architectures where each service could be replaced quickly. At an architecture symposium in the Lake District, England, James pitched a name for this trend: “micro apps,” and in a room of about 10 people (including Sam), someone else suggested “microservices.” Lewis and Martin Fowler then wrote the first article on the topic in March 2014, ‘Microservices: a definition of this new architectural term’, and Sam published the book Building Microservices the following year.

2. Sam spent 18 months teaching Googlers how to write good automated tests. In 2007, Sam was embedded at Yahoo and Google as a ThoughtWorks consultant, alongside people from Pivotal Labs. Their job was to teach engineers how to write automated tests, and code that’s testable. He recalls that some Google devs did not believe it was possible to write automated functional tests for websites, until Sam and his colleagues showed them how Selenium works!

3. Sam spent 10+ years at a large company, three years at startups, and has been independent for more than a decade. After 13 years at Thoughtworks, he quit to avoid becoming “institutionalized.” He recalls thinking he could hang around at Thoughtworks and grow bitter. “So I’ll just go now.” He then worked at three different startups before going independent, which he’s now done for 15 years. The biggest challenge of being your own boss? He says: “The problem of working for yourself is that the boss is frequently an a*****e. So, current Sam frequently is cursing past Sam for the commitments he made!”

4. So, what’s a “microservice?” Sam gives two definitions: a clear one, and a softer one:

  1. Independently deployable service. The “clear” definition: as long as, upon a change to a system, it can be independently deployed – without any other services needing to be deployed –, you can call it a microservice.

  2. Clear boundaries around the business domain. The “softer” definition: services split by business function (not by technical layer) can also be called microservices.

5. Three rules of distributed systems: Sam sometimes struggled to recall the eight fallacies of distributed computing, and so he boiled them down to the three that cause the most problems:

1. Information takes time to travel. You cannot send information instantaneously from point A to point B. This is basically the “speed of light” constraint.

2. Sometimes, the thing you want to talk to isn’t there. That is, resources can and do go offline.

3. Resources are not infinite; you will eventually run out of things like CPU, memory, storage, and networking bandwidth.

In Sam’s experience, most distributed systems outages are caused by #3; resource pools running out.

6. Dealing with idempotency: keys or fingerprints? Idempotency is performing the same operation multiple times and it having the same effect as if done once only. For example, if you repeatedly hit the “down” button for an elevator, nothing more happens than what happened upon that first press: multiple button smashes don’t bring more elevators your way. Payments are a classic example where idempotency is needed: when you retry or refresh a payments page, you should not be charged twice.

There are two common ways to deal with idempotency:

  • Idempotency keys: a client sends a unique identifier (usually a UUID) that is the idempotency key. The server makes sure operations with the same idempotency key are executed only once. It’s clean to build but hard to retrofit, which involves changing both the client and server.

  • Fingerprints: the client sends nothing, but the server creates a “fingerprint” of the request by hashing relevant fields. It’s easy to retrofit later (only need to change the server), however, legitimate requests can be rejected as duplicates, and duplicate requests could still happen. Sam describes a Danish payment system he worked on that rejected purchases of the same value within a 5-minute period while it did the fingerprinting.

7. Four concepts of resiliency: Sam frequently references the four outcomes for military systems, explained by David Woods:

  • Robustness: systems continue to function as intended, for example, when Kubernetes replaces a failing pod. A downside of robustness is that it can add complexity, and more complex systems have more ways to fail.

  • Rebound: how quickly the system recovers when something goes wrong.

  • Extensibility: dealing with surprises and being able to stretch the system’s support to deal with new needs

  • Adaptability: the system changing to support new functions. Resilient systems are adapted, even between incidents.

8. What if code is a side effect of collaboration? When Sam was at Thoughtworks, some clients refused to do pair programming as a practice because they could only see one developer typing and the other doing nothing, which is a waste. Martin Fowler’s dictum that “programming is not typing” helped Sam to explain to clients that typing out code is an output, but not an outcome.

Sam conceives programming as building a system collectively, and code is one of the mechanisms delivering the system. Now that with LLMs we no longer spend most time typing out code, we’ll discover the next bottleneck in creating good software. Could it be delayed feedback cycles?

9. Hedging the vendor options is sensible when integrating AI into systems. It’s hard to tell which AI companies have long-term, sustainable business models and which don’t, so it’s the responsible thing when designing systems to hedge the providers. Aim to be multi-vendor, multi-model in your choices, so you can easily change the vendor or model layer. Also, consider if you can swap out LLM-powered functionality for deterministic code that runs faster and cheaper.

10. We must resist “cognitive surrender” to AI. Sam believes that more AI usage is leading to less critical thinking – or could we be using it wrong? He says: “The original pitch of AI was it was going to free us from drudgery. We’d have less toil, and we can focus more on critical thinking and smarts. However, much of our current use of AI is not freeing us up from critical thinking! It’s causing more context switching and leaving less time for thinking. People are working longer hours; we’ve got studies that show this.

But [longer hours and more context switching] is not necessarily AI’s fault. It’s just how we’re using it.”

Putting in the effort often leads to better results. For example, when writing Building Resilient Distributed Systems, Sam used NotebookLM for research, but he manually clicked through each link it surfaced, and checked whether it was information he wanted to reference.

11. Starting with modules encourages better software architecture. Also: production is truth. I asked Sam for advice on what to do to get better at designing systems:

  • Start by thinking carefully about module boundaries and the connections between them

  • When you use AI, allow it to roam freely, but only inside the module structure that you have designed!

12. Much of the tech world might still be naive about what an LLM is. As Sam said:

“I think the tech world in general is quite naive about AI and fundamentally misunderstands what an LLM is. For example: why did the LLM delete my database? Well, because it has no concept of causality. They have no concept that if I do A, B happens.

LLMs are not world models. World models have been around for a long time. They predate LLMs. So if you had the appropriate model and the appropriate inputs, world models could at least get to the point of ‘if I do X, then Y happens and I’ve been told not to do Y.’

I think we expect LLMs to do more than they actually can do, because they seem so smart. This leads us to overestimate their capabilities a bit too much. But the nature of LLMs is why all the guardrails around LLMs are really not going to be the right long-term solution.”

Sam’s comments feel very timely, given Opus 5.5 just formatted the hard drive of a dev who ran the model with the —dangerously-skip-permissions tag, and was surprised to see all of his data gone.

Finally, recommended reading to get better at software architecture. Sam’s recommendations:

  • Fundamentals of Software Architecture by Neal Ford and Mark Richards.

  • Balanced Coupling by Vlad Khononov

  • On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules: a paper by David Parnas from the 1970s original papers from the early 1970s, such as

  • An architecturally-evident coding style: making your design visible: a paper by George Fairbanks, published in 2010. It’s an approach that allows the code to hint at the system’s architecture

The Pragmatic Engineer deepdives relevant for this episode

• The past and future of modern backend practices

• What is reliability engineering, and the history of SRE

title: The state of the tech industry in 2026
feed_text:
I recently delivered the keynote at the LDX3 engineering leadership conference in New York, attended by 2,000+ engineering leaders, CTOs, Director+ and Staff+ engineering folks, in which I attempted to create a snapshot of where the tech industry is at this exact point.

It came after I had the chance to visit the AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic, meet innovative startups like Ramp, Uber and others, get new, unpublished data from GitHub, Factory AI and Linear. The focus of the talk is trend inside of AI labs, VC-funded startups and Big Tech. Thanks to the kind access to these teams!

Before the conference, I spent weeks identifying and recording trends that didn’t exist a year ago – or were much more nascent back then – and also things that are currently broken, and others that remain unchanged. Today, we cover:

  1. Speed of change. In the tech industry, change has never been this large-scale, this fast. Industry legend Martin Fowler confirms.

  2. What’s changed: practically nobody writes code by hand anymore, working with 5-10 agents more common, the fading of the IDE, and 13 more changes from the last year.

  3. What’s broken: assumptions about code output broke, code reviews became theatrical, quality and reliability is down, and more.

  4. What’s still the same: teams are still important, as is planning; non-engineers are still not shipping code, and more.

  5. What comes next? Cloud coding agents and harnesses, engineers to stop reading the code, companies building a new type of AI infra, and more are already starting, and should accelerate.

You can watch the full talk, which is 29 minutes long:

Watch the full talk

Paid subscribers can also access the slides for the presentation:

This post has bonus content for paid subscribers. Upgrade to get full access.

1. Speed of change

People in tech are more than used to change; seeing the internet go from zero to everywhere, the arrival of mobile communications and smartphones exploding in popularity, cloud computing rising from a niche concern, and the development of programming languages like Go and Rust, and frameworks like React (web) and Jetpack Compose (Android).

Despite this, the scale and pace of the impact AI is having at present is still without precedent. That’s how industry veteran Martin Fowler described it at The Pragmatic Summit:

“Nothing has hit with the magnitude of AI. This is a whole size difference from anything that we’ve faced before.

On a smaller scale, we were very much involved in the growth of object-oriented languages. [object-oriented languages] scared a lot of people, but it didn’t scare us so much because we were part of it.

The internet had a huge impact upon us all. And, of course, we were spreading the challenge of agile software development. [Agile] had a very big impact on a lot of organizations because you could tell by how hard they resisted it.

But [for all those other changes] we kept talking about how important they were and how valuable they were and trying to persuade people of the importance of them. It may sound surprising, but even for the internet, there were people who wouldn’t think that was important!

For AI there’s no argument about how important it is. You cannot put blinkers on to deny the importance of this thing.”

My own take is similar; we are without doubt at the beginning of a massive technological transformation, and after it, software will be built differently from how we’ve been doing for decades, although some parts of development will remain the same. At the very least, the tooling and best practices will look different, and things are changing faster than ever.

2. What’s changed?

#1 Nobody writes code by hand anymore

As the calendar enters Q4 of this year, we see this has solidified into a mega trend since the end of 2025 year when models greatly improved at coding. Related to this, in the very first article of this year we asked the question: when AI writes almost all code, what happens to software engineering?

Today, there are plenty of signs that most engineers have stopped writing code by hand, and it was also a sign of the times recently when the Ruby on Rails creator sparked a “death of coding by hand” debate. Personally, I’m excited by the new opportunity that AI creates, and it’s exciting to experience this revolution firsthand. As mentioned in that deepdive, I’m certain that my way of coding will change drastically in 2026, and there’ll be plenty of knock-on effects.

For more on this topic, check out this recent edition of The Pulse.

#2 Working with several parallel agents is increasingly common

I like talking to engineers at AI labs because their working practices are often a few months ahead of the rest of the industry. Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny, revealed the new way he gets things done on the podcast:

“I have 5 terminal tabs. Each one of them has a checkout of their repository. I’ll round robin and start Claude Code in each one. I also run 5-10 Claudes on Claude Web, in parallel with my local Claudes.”

A few months after these comments, on last week’s pod with Cockroach Labs cofounder, Peter Mattis, – who’s an extremely productive developer who wrote circa 100K lines of code/year, pre-AI – said he’s doing something similar:

“Oftentimes, I’m doing things in parallel. I find my cognitive overhead is about 5-10 agent sessions concurrently. But sometimes those sessions will have many subagents doing things.”

I also asked a former coworker at Uber, who’s also an extremely productive software engineer, how he works these days. Dima Zaytsev (now a software engineer at Linear), told me:

“⁠It used to be a simple world: one mouse, one keyboard, one screen. You physically can’t work on more than one thing at once. Now, you no longer have that limitation.

I end up having 5-10 (literally) worktrees locally that I rotate between. Prompt one agent, and while it is working, move on to another to test output or review code.”

Nearly all of the most productive software engineers I’ve met – who were hand-writing code a year ago – no longer write the code by hand and also run several parallel agents. What a change!

#3 Rapid rise of agent-generated PRs

Fresh data that GitHub shared with me:

I’ve given GitHub grief for its ongoing reliability issues, but seeing how rapidly agent-generated PRs are growing makes me a lot more empathetic for the load which the platform is dealing with.

Food for thought: there were more agent-authored PRs in August 2026 on GitHub than human-authored ones! It’s reasonable to speculate that the number of agent-generated PRs will be permanently exceeding human-generated ones on the platform, going forward.

To give a sense of the number of AI-generated PRs: as of today (October 2025), there is likely to be 3x as many fully AI-generated PRs, per month (probably 75M+), than human generated ones at the end of 2023 (25M in December 2023). And the pace of AI-generated PRs does not seem to be slowing down, at least not now.

#4 Agent-generated issues also rising rapidly

Agents are not just generating PRs, they’re also opening tickets. Some more exclusive data, this time from my friends at Linear, which added first-class MCP support for agentic creation of issues:

#5 Agent skills usage is mainstream

Both engineers and non-engineers use agent skills, and lots of companies are building their own agent skills repositories for all staff to create, share, and evaluate. An interesting data point on skills usage trending heavily up comes from autonomous software factory vendor Factory AI, which shared with me:

#6 The fading IDE

I have great respect for software engineer Steve Yegge, who’s good at identifying emerging trends and learning about them. In a podcast episode, he said the IDE is effectively over:

Gergely: “Speaking about the job as developers, you’ve said something that can be triggering for a lot of people. You’ve said, on the AI Engineer Summit, that if you’re still using an IDE now, you’re a bad engineer.”

Steve: “Yeah, well, you got to be a little provocative. Let me put it this way. Okay, I’m not going to say you’re a bad engineer because I know some very, very good engineers, better than I am, who are still at level one or two in my chart [of AI usage]? But I feel profoundly sorry for them.

I feel pity for them like I’ve never felt in my life. For these grown people who are good engineers or used to be. And they’re like, ‘yeah, you know, I use Cursor and I ask it questions sometimes. And I’m really impressed with the answers. And then I review its code really carefully.’

And then I check it in and I’m like: ‘dude, you’re going to get fired. And you’re one of the best engineers I know!!’ “

Steve described his levels of AI usage like this:

  1. No AI usage

  2. AI agent in the IDE, with strict permissions

  3. AI agent in the IDE, with “YOLO” mode (permissions off)

  4. AI agent in the IDE, no longer looking at the code, but interacting with the agent

  5. CLI-first: abandoned the IDE

  6. Running several agents in parallel

  7. Running 10+ agents

  8. Built a custom agent orchestrator to run 30+ (or 100+) agents

Steve believes that “AI-pilled” engineers will abandon the IDE, and I’m seeing data from the market which backs that prediction:

  • Antigravity 1.0 was the last IDE released, based on a VS Code fork. It was released in November 2025. After that, no major IDE that is a VS Code Fork has launched. In May 2026, when Antigravity 2.0 launched, the product moved away from the IDE concept.

  • Codex launched as a non-IDE in Feb 2026, and they’re glad they did so, despite being torn about moving away from the IDE concept, at the end of 2025.

  • Cursor moved away from the IDE. In April 2026, Cursor relaunched and got rid of the IDE interface. It now looks pretty similar to the Codex and Claude desktop apps. When I talked to their team over the summer, they told me they maintain the “legacy” VS Code fork version for existing enterprises, but the future is agentic for them.

  • JetBrains seems in a hurry to pivot from IDEs. JetBrains has built some of the most beloved IDEs for developers, but the company is now also pivoting to JetBrains Air, and agentic development environments.

Industry legend Kent Beck told me something interesting when we discussed why IDEs are slowly vanishing:

“It’s not that we don’t need more perspective and context for our human-based decisions; it’s that the context has changed.”

I wonder if what is really happening is the IDE evolving into something different to work better with coding agents. Steve Yegge also talked about how the IDE needs to evolve into a conversation and monitoring interface, but not an editor, given that we no longer write the code.

I’d also add that IDEs need to evolve into a validation and verification interface: how do we know that the agents’ output works as expected, how can we verify what tests it passes, how it looks, and whether you can try out whatever the agent builds. Tools like this are surely coming and will be widely adopted.

#7 Everyone is building their own harness/agent platform

In August, I posed a question on social media about whether it’s possible to be a serious tech business without having built an AI harness:

I asked it because most mid-sized-and-above companies have built their own agent harnesses, at this point! A few examples:

  • Ramp building Inspect – a case study we covered in depth

  • Stripe (Minions), Uber (Minion), Block (Goose), Shopify (River)

  • Google (Agent Smith), Meta (Devmate), Amazon (Kiro + Crew), Dropbox (Nova), Spotify (Honk)

  • DoorDash (Flux), Grab (LLM-Kit), WorkOS (Horizon), Hubspot (Crucible)

  • Monzo (Agent Chip), Sierra (Pinecone), Harvey (Spectre), Browserbase (bb)

  • … and many, many more!

#8 Dev work often starts in Slack

What I’ve learned by visiting startups is that more and more development kicks off inside Slack. At OpenAI, it’s “@Codex, implement this”; within Anthropic, it’s “@Claude build this”, while inside Linear, it’s “@Linear work on this”. More startups have their own Slack integration of their coding agent – often a custom one.

Coding agents work really well when deeply integrated into a company’s stack, when the Slack agent kicks off a coding agent that runs in the cloud.

#9 Agentic software factories being built everywhere

We have covered in-depth how OpenAI is building an agentic software factory, and a lot of feedback from readers about that article has been an “we are too!” type response. Many readers say that their company is building a similar “agentic software factory.”

The “agentic software factory” adds AI functionality to a bunch of existing systems such as the CI/CD system; for instance, in being able to interact with CI/CD via Slack, or creating brand new systems with agents in them like agentic code review tools, OpenAI’s agentic deploy system, or the Perf Factory.

#10 Migrations no longer take years

We’re seeing many migrations that would have taken years to complete, now taking mere weeks or months:

  • Anthropic: migrating the package manager Bun from Zig to Rust in 11 days (versus an estimated 1.5 engineering years)

  • OpenAI: the API layer is being migrated from Python to Rust. The migration is taking around 5 months, versus several years that it would have taken, without AI

  • Airbnb: migrating 3,500 end-to-end test files from Enzyme to React Testing Library: took 6 weeks (instead of years)

  • Asana: migrating 4,000 end-to-end test files from Enzyme to React Testing Library: 2 weeks, instead of an estimated spread out over five years

  • Uber: migrating 600,000 JUnit 4 tests across 15 million lines of code (!!) to JUnit 5: took 4 months (instead of estimated several years)

#11 AI costs a major engineering concern

In May, we covered the trend of companies wanting to cut back on AI spend within engineering departments, and last month, I reported on how tech companies are moving to open AI models to save 50% or more in token costs. Uber is a good example, where, despite token usage trending upwards, costs have stayed flat since May thanks to them running open models and doing smart model routing:

Three weeks after my article, Bloomberg confirmed the exact same trend. As I covered in my original deepdive, lower-cost models and smart routing account for the majority of cost savings at most companies. If you’re only doing two things, consider those techniques.

#12 Projects get done with only one or two engineers

Katelyn Lesse, Head of Engineering for Claude Platform, told me how her team works inside Anthropic. From our deepdive:

“On an individual project, you often cannot have more than two people working on it. This is because each engineer is already running several agents. And so as an engineer, you’re already fighting against your agents, which are stepping on each other’s toes on implementation. And in this setup, you just cannot have that many humans, who also come with all their agents!”

These days, I see the same thing happening at companies both small and large.

Other changes

  • 13. Engineering specializations are disappearing. Specifically, there seems to be less demand for iOS, Android, and frontend specializations, and more for “generic” software engineers. We covered this trend with data in the State of the software engineering job market in 2026, observing how mobile and frontend demand is dropping (while AI & FDE demand surges)

  • 14. Teams are getting smaller. Projects are being done by fewer engineers. Inside startups, team sizes seem to be shrinking.

  • 15. Reduced junior recruitment. We cover how it’s harder for graduates & interns to get hired in the State of the software engineering job market in 2026 deepdive.

  • 16. Agentic infra is becoming its own discipline. Most mid-sized-and-above companies are building out agentic platforms, and infra teams are increasingly morphing into agentic infra teams.

3. What’s broken?

Assumptions about code quantity and frequency

It’s been a commonly held belief that code quantity grows roughly linearly. But with agents, both the lines of code and number of commits are growing exponentially, as shown in data from GitHub:

(Human) code reviews are dead

A software engineer at a mid-sized startup told me something that’s pretty much an open secret across the industry, including at places with code reviews in place.

“Everyone is playing the theater of doing reviews, but with the volume of changes that get thrown your way, I observed that people just find a path of least resistance: give up on reviews and just stamp everything with LGTM.

We are gradually phasing out this process ourselves with some shortcuts that you are allowed to take, and that has been a major productivity boost.”

At the LDX3 conference, there was a strong reaction among the audience when they heard the bolded sentence out above. Today at most companies, there is indeed a “theater of code reviews”. The fact is that no engineer can keep up with 5-10 times more code to review, so most don’t thoroughly review the code.

Agent-only code reviews trending up

Fresh data from Linear shows that PRs which are reviewed solely by AI agents are a rising trend, and I expect it’ll continue:

Quality and reliability down

We see this in many of the digital products we use. As Mario Zechner, the creator of Pi, said on the podcast:

“Everything is broken. It sure feels like software has become a brittle mess, with 98% uptime becoming the norm instead of the exception, including for big services. And user interfaces have the weirdest bugs that you’d think a QA team would catch. I give you that that’s been the case for longer than agents exist. But we seem to be accelerating.”

We covered the phenomenon of quality being worse with more AI usage in March, in ‘Are AI agents actually slowing us down?’

Infra capacity shortage

It’s common knowledge that there’s a GPU shortage and memory shortage in the market. In addition, there’s also the growing trend of CPU shortages. As I covered last month:

“Apparently, it’s now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Also, reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance, and cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don’t have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.”

If you’re at a company with a non-trivial amount of CPU usage, securing capacity is something worth doing now, as I wrote recently:

“The best time to secure more CPU capacity is most certainly right now. I’m hearing rumors that certain cloud regions no longer accept new tenants because all CPU capacity is leased, or negotiations elsewhere are difficult. I’m also hearing that customers are already paying today to reserve capacity that will only come online in data centers from December. This seems predatory by providers, but demand is so high that this is how they likely prioritize new capacity allocation – while earning much higher profits than usual.

If your company has dynamic workloads, and you’ve used spot instances in the past, now could be a good time to allocate fixed capacity – even if it’s more expensive. If you expect meaningful growth, doing so now might mean having options at some cloud providers or in some regions.”

A hit on personal focus and productivity

Software engineer Dima Zaytsev (currently at Linear, formerly my colleague at Uber) told me something that felt very relatable on AI and productivity:

“There’s lots of context switching: there’s always another agent that waits on your response.

Also, it’s just more work. When AI was ramping up, I felt more productive than my peers: I did in an hour what others needed a day for. Now, the expectation has become that everyone works on parallel things. And so, I end up feeling I have more work compared to pre-AI.”

Engineering leaders taking career breaks

An interesting, unexpected trend that has emerged is CTOs, Heads of Engineering, and VPs of Engineering resigning from their jobs, often with nothing specific lined up. From a current CTO who asked to remain anonymous:

“This change [with AI] makes builders want to build. We want to build again, so we can build more, and build faster with better tools, so we can increase the “talent density” of the team by doing more with fewer great people, and so on.

It’s an amazing time to build things. And it’s only getting better. And people just want to be close to it. They want to build and see how far they can go with these new tools.

I have a bunch of friends in my social circle who are the “CTO drop outs” you speak of. More still who are moving from management to IC roles in large companies. And their stories are largely what I describe above. They simply see this as a truly exciting time to build.

In the end, building is why they got into this field in the first place.”

We cover this in the deepdive ‘Headed for the exit: the great engineering leader career break’.

4. What’s still the same?

In the LDX3 keynote, I also covered areas that are mostly unchanged from before AI:

Teams are still important. As Katelyn Lesse, Head of Engineering for Claude Platform told me in July:

“One thing I’ve heard from some people is “we have two humans and a bunch of agents.” I reply that this isn’t where we’re at. I still have teams whose job it is to own a piece of software, iterate on it, own oncall, and so on. While each of these humans are supercharged by AI, the size and shape of the team is still similar. We still have two-pizza teams.”

Katelyn works at one of the most “AI-pilled” companies globally, so if teams are still as important there as they were before AI, then it’s not a stretch to say that the team structure is still relevant at companies across the industry.

Planning still happens – at least for complex work. Complex projects still have a lengthy planning phase. Also from Katelyn, on the planning phase of Claude Managed Agents:

“Our planning process looked more like a typical pre-AI planning process. You know how every team has the project, where everyone comes up with some version of the same idea and people keep floating and circling it around until you finally do it? Managed Agents was this for our team. When we started the project, we had documents dating back up to two years about ideas and suggestions.”

Tests and validation are still very important. From Jarred Sumner, creator of Bun, who’s currently at Anthropic:

“The AI writes pretty much all the code, but we have the AI write pretty much all the tests as well. Before AI, for production-ready software, we spent about the same time writing tests as we did on writing code. This is still the case with AI. You need to have a way to trust your code, and tests are probably the best way to.”

At each company I talked to in advance of the LDX3 keynote, I observed that a lot of focus is going into validating the output of AI agents. This makes sense: code review no longer works like it did before, we have more code, and we need to make sure that it won’t break production!

Non-engineers are still not shipping prod code. In the last few weeks, there’s been stuff on social media about AI enabling product managers/designers/non-technical people to ship production code. So, I asked the AI labs, startups, and other companies.

I can report that I did not find any single company where PMs/designers/non-technical people ship to production!

What I did learn about are cases where these folks create bugfixes – often unknowingly! – or new features with their agents that end up with devs to review. There’s also a massive amount of prototyping. But it’s still engineers who are responsible for deciding what can and what cannot be released to production.

We’re rediscovering old patterns that work great with AI. This came up in our podcast with Matt Pocock. Matt noticed that agents try to build software layer by layer, which causes bugs between the layers. Reading The Pragmatic Programmer, he discovered the concept of the “tracer bullet.” When he instructed the agent to use “tracer bullets” to build an app (aka implement a “golden path”), the agent started to produce better code.

As mentioned in the podcast, Matt is now reading classic software engineering books to find other “leading words” that guide agents efficiently.

In general, I’m noticing that “old” best practices are helpful when building better software when working with AI. This includes writing unit tests, building a “golden path” first (aka a “tracer bullet”), architecting an application upfront, and even using design patterns. The amusing thing is that we’re talking about decades-old best practices here.

5. What comes next?

It’s possible to look ahead at where the tech industry is headed by identifying trends that are underway, and which look certain to conitnue:

Cloud coding agents + harnesses will dominate. Most devs at companies will run AI agents in the cloud, instead of locally. Ramp offers a blueprint for this in our deepdive about their cloud agent, called Inspect. It seems that inside innovative tech companies, the “build your own cloud agent harness” principle is trending.

I also expect vendors like Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX, and others to start pushing their cloud coding agent offerings, and for more startups to build their own cloud harnesses.

As engineers, we’ll stop reading the code. It’s too early to tell when this will happen; this year, next year, or further in the future, but it’s likely that few of us will read the code that AI agents produce properly, going forward.

As a rule, I pay a lot of attention to Honeycomb cofounder and CTO, Charity Majors, due to her being a “default sceptic” about new technology, as well as a standout engineer and someone who speaks her mind. On our podcast in August, she asked:

“What would it take for you to be comfortable shipping code without you reading it and understanding it? Because that is engineering.”

Charity made the point that Ops and QA have already had decades to figure out how to ship code to production that they didn’t write and don’t understand – all while making sure it works! It seems unavoidable that most software engineers will also join this group. This is ironic, since software engineering, for the longest time, was about engineers writing and understanding the code!

Companies will build brand new types of internal infra. We’ll see a “reinvention” of these systems to work well with agents:

  • CI/CD, with agentic evals part of the pipelines

  • Agentic software factories, and figuring out what is and isn’t practical

  • Agents becoming part of deployments, observability, incident management

  • Agentic observability will surely become its own problem space and specialization: how can we make sure the customer-facing agents deployed work as expected, and how to ensure that systems which agents build and modify actually work as expected?

A “golden age” of refactoring/migrations/full-on rewrites. Migrations and rewrites that had been delayed for years because they’d take similar amounts of time to complete, should take no longer than weeks. That means there’s little excuse to delay any longer!

Engineers understand more about how capable AI agents are with rewrites/refactors/migrations today, and we’ll also clean up tech debt much faster, while having no reason to have a system in a state that we’re unhappy with!

AI “fluency” and “positivity” matter in recruitment at startups. A trend I have not written much about – but which is already happening – is startups selecting engineers for jobs who demonstrate a positive attitude about AI. As the Director of Engineering at a Series D startup told me:

“AI positivity was something we started to screen for in our hiring process. We want people to join who want to help us push the limits with what we can build with AI.”

The reality is that AI coding agents are already everywhere, and agentic systems look set to proliferate very soon. This will bring great demand for software engineers who are willing and able to build next-generation systems, and it’ll be a baseline criterion to be excited about the problem space.

This is not too dissimilar to the way that startups hire engineers who buy into the idea of growing fast, or when companies favor engineers who pick up the tech stack already in use, instead of insisting upon the one that they personally use.

Engineers with deep domain knowledge will become more in demand. In New York, I had a conversation with Titus Winters, lead author of Software Engineering at Google. He told me this observation:

“What you need to succeed anywhere is intelligence, wisdom, and charisma. Intelligence means: how to do it. Wisdom means: what to do. Charisma means: convince others to do it.

When intelligence becomes commonplace, wisdom and charisma become much more important.”

In the context of software engineering, “wisdom” is most easily earned by becoming a domain expert. So, if you work at a fintech company, learn about the finance industry and its customers in order to become a more valuable, in-demand engineer! That also applies if you’re at an agriculture tech company, or work in any other domain.

Finally: remind yourself why you got into the tech industry. At the end of my podcast with Peter Mattis, the cofounder and CTO of Cockroach Labs, we talked about how it feels pretty exhausting right now to keep up with the pace of change. He said:

“Remind yourself why you got into this in the first place. I got into software engineering because I like building stuff. Now I can build faster, and without some of the compromises that I had before!”

title: The Pulse: Firebase’s global outage & poor response
feed_text:
The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover:

  1. Firebase: global outage & poor handling by Google. The Firebase iOS SDK crashed after a backend change, crashing all apps which used Firebase analytics for 2-6 hours. Google did not update the status page or offer any postmortem, which is a head-scratcher from a company known for standout incident management practices.

  2. OpenAI’s platform play from AWS playbook? OpenAI is becoming a platform where it’s possible to allocate ChatGPT spend on open models and AI offerings from among 16 partners, not just OpenAI models. It’s fair to ask if Anthropic will consider a similar platform play.

  3. More data on companies moving to open models. Vercel’s AI gateway shows 60% of model spend goes to open weight models, and OpenRouter also shows open models are being more used than closed ones.

  4. Why CTOs and VPEs are quitting en masse: another take. What if it’s not “founder mode”, but about people who love building software, feeling like they can do it solo (or with a small team) with AI tools?
